chunks.title: Motion Director — Overview
chunks.text:
Motion Director (/studio/motion-director). Overview.
description: Chat with an AI director that plans a storyboard for a product film (using your website's real pages if you give a link), builds it from motion shot cards, and lets you render an MP4 or keep editing in the Motion Workbench.
shortDescription: Chat with an AI director that plans a storyboard for a product film (using your website's real pages if you give a link), builds it from motion shot cards, and lets you render an MP4 or keep editing in the Motion Workbench.
fullDescription: Motion Director opens on a chat page. You describe the film you want (a message with a site address makes the film use real pages from that site), choose an aspect ratio, optionally attach images, videos or audio, optionally pick shot cards from Templates, and click Generate. The director then asks how to proceed (use the Ink Press template, let the director pick shots, choose shot cards, or work it out together step by step), writes a storyboard for you to read, and builds the film only after you click Approve & build film. The finished film plays in the chat with buttons to render an MP4, render a fast draft, render without music, or open the film in the Motion Workbench, an editor with a timeline, an inspector, a library of shots, sounds and themes, and an Edit agent chat. Work is kept in this browser; a film or project saved earlier in the old Motion Studio shows up here too.

chunks.title: Motion Director — Overview
chunks.text:
Motion Director (/studio/motion-director). Overview.
bestFor: Marketing teams and founders who want an editable promotional film made from their own site.
whenToUse:
- Making a product or launch film from a website
- Producing a polished short film with real pages
- Editing a built film on a timeline
- Trying different shot styles quickly
whenToUseAnother:
- Use Video Studio for AI-generated video clips
- Use Storyboard to plan scenes and frames
- Use Design Agent for static designs
- Use Vibe Motion for motion graphics
businessValue: Turns a link and a short brief into an editable film without a video team.

chunks.title: Motion Director — How to use
chunks.text:
Motion Director (/studio/motion-director). How to use.
howToUse: Open Motion Director from the studio list (/studio/motion-director); the chat page opens. Type what film you want (include your site link to use its real pages), choose the aspect ratio, optionally attach files or pick shot cards in Templates, and click Generate. Answer the director's question, read the storyboard, click Approve & build film, then render the MP4 or open the film in the Motion Workbench.
howToSteps:
- Open Motion Director from the studio list. You see the heading Films are easier with Motion Director and a message box.
- Optional: click Brand Kit to add your business name, colours and logos (it turns into Brand Kit · On once a brand is selected). Optional: click the + button (Attach image / video / audio) to add pictures, videos or music.
- Type your request in the box, for example Create a 30-second promotional film from my website... (put your site address in the message to use its real pages, and say the length you want in the message, like 30 seconds; if you do not say, 20 seconds is used). Choose the aspect ratio with the 16:9 button (the menu offers 16:9, 9:16 and 1:1).
- Optional: click Templates, search with Search recipes..., open a category chip, and click a shot card to add it. You can pick several; they appear as chips next to Templates and the film uses them in order.

chunks.title: Motion Director — How to use
chunks.text:
Motion Director (/studio/motion-director). How to use.
- Click the send button, which is labelled Generate for a new film. If you gave no template or shot names, the director replies with a question: click Use Ink Press, Let the director pick shots, Choose shot cards…, or Work it out together.
- If you chose Work it out together, the director first runs a Product check and asks you to confirm. Click Looks right — next (or answer in your own words), then pick a visual direction with Use A, Use B or Use C (or Use my recommendation), then check the feature-to-shot map and click Looks right — write the storyboard. You can click You decide at any step to let the director choose the rest.
- Wait while the progress strip runs. A button ■ Stop cancels storyboarding or building at any time.
- Read the storyboard card (scenes, lengths, and whether it uses your site). To change it, type what to change in the message box or click Revise; to accept it, click Approve & build film.
- When the film is ready, a FINAL FILM card appears with a player. Click Render MP4 to make the file (the page must stay open), or Fast draft for a smaller quicker version, or Render without music if the film has a music track. When rendering finishes click Download MP4.
- To edit shots, copy, timing and sound, click Open in Motion Workbench. Use Back to chat to return; the film stays under Continue editing.

chunks.title: Motion Director — How to use
chunks.text:
Motion Director (/studio/motion-director). How to use.
- To start another film, click ↺ New film or type a new request.
gettingStarted:
- Open Motion Director from the studio list.
- Write what film you want and include your site link if you have one.
- Click Generate and choose Use Ink Press when asked (the quickest path).
- Read the storyboard and click Approve & build film.
- Click Render MP4 and then Download MP4.
tips:
- Put your site address in the message: the film then shows your real pages and logo. Without one the director uses sample pages.
- Say the length in your message (for example 30 seconds). Films are planned between 5 and 90 seconds and 2 to 14 scenes.
- Use the Templates picker to force specific shot cards; up to 12 can be chosen.
- Reply to the director in plain words: say looks right, you decide, or name what to change.
- Use Fast draft while experimenting; render the full size at the end.
- Keep the tab open while an MP4 renders; closing or reloading cancels it.
bestPractices:
- Give the director a clear product name and a link; answer the product check honestly because later steps use it.
- Review the storyboard card before approving; revising is cheaper than rebuilding the film.
- Attach your own music if you want cuts on its beat; the progress strip says when no music is attached.
- After building, open the Motion Workbench for fine edits instead of starting a new film.

chunks.title: Motion Director — How to use
chunks.text:
Motion Director (/studio/motion-director). How to use.
- Render the MP4 on a computer with enough memory; very long or heavy films take longer (the card shows a rough minutes estimate).

troubleshooting:
- Nothing happens when I click Generate: Make sure there is text in the box (or a picked shot card).

- Message starting 'Could not capture': The film continues with sample pages. Check that the link is a public site.
- MP4 render fails or says the browser cannot encode MP4: Use a current Chrome or Edge on a computer.

- Generation is blocked by keys: If generation is blocked, open the API keys settings and check your keys.

Motion Director (/studio/motion-director). Problems and limits.
- question: Do I need a website? | answer: No. Without a link the film uses sample pages; a link or attached screenshots make it use your real pages.
- question: How do I set the length? | answer: Say it in the message (for example 30 seconds). The default is 20 seconds.
- question: What does Work it out together do? | answer: It runs a Product check, proposes visual directions and a feature-to-shot map, and waits for your confirmation at each step before writing the storyboard.
- question: How do I change the storyboard? | answer: Type what to change in the box or click Revise.
- question: How do I get an MP4? | answer: Click Render MP4 on the FINAL FILM card (or Export video in the Workbench), wait, then click Download MP4.
- question: What happens if I leave while rendering? | answer: The render is cancelled; the studio asks you to confirm first.
- question: Where is Continue editing? | answer: Under Recent Projects. It also shows a project recovered from the old Motion Studio.
- question: Can I use my own music? | answer: Yes. Attach an audio file with the + button before generating.
- question: How many shots can I choose? | answer: Up to 12 shot cards per film.
- question: Can I publish the film? | answer: After an export in the Workbench, click Post to social.

chunks.title: SmartVideo GO AI Apps — Overview
chunks.text:
SmartVideo GO AI Apps (/studio/apps). Overview.
description: The Reseller Studio marketplace: browse the collection of ready-made AI apps, open live demos, read deployment guides, get the source code, deploy to Vercel and follow the launch walkthrough. Also shows the two reseller packages.
shortDescription: Browse the SmartVideo GO AI app collection, try live demos, open deployment guides and source code, and compare the reseller packages.
fullDescription: SmartVideo GO AI Apps is the reseller marketplace page (route /studio/apps). Its top section introduces the reseller program and links to the Reseller Deployment Center. Under 'Choose How You Build' it shows two packages: 'DIY App Builder' ($197 one-time) and 'Apps + Training' ($597 one-time), each with a button that opens Stripe Checkout in a new tab, plus an upgrade button for the $400 difference. 'How It Works' explains the three steps (Choose Your App, Customize & Build, Launch Your Business) and links to the 'Reseller Setup Walkthrough'. Below that, 'The Application Collection' lists app cards you can search and filter by category. Each card can offer 'Try Live Demo', 'Deployment Guide', 'Source Code', 'Deploy on Vercel' and 'Learn How to Launch This App'. This studio does not generate media; it is a catalogue and a route to deployment and training.
bestFor: People who want to launch their own AI software business from ready-made apps.

howToUse: Open /studio/apps, search or filter for an app, then use the buttons on its card: 'Try Live Demo', 'Deployment Guide', 'Source Code', 'Deploy on Vercel' or 'Learn How to Launch This App'. Use 'Reseller Setup Walkthrough' for the full guided course.
howToSteps:
- Open SmartVideo GO AI Apps at /studio/apps (choose 'SmartVideo GO AI Apps' in the studio list). The top of the page shows the 'SMARTVIDEO AI APPS RESELLER PROGRAM' banner with the headline 'Your Apps. Your Brand. Your Business.'. The button 'Open the Reseller Deployment Center' opens the full deployment documentation at /reseller/deployment.
- Read the two package cards under 'Choose How You Build': 'DIY App Builder' ($197, one-time, button 'Get All Apps') and 'Apps + Training' ($597, one-time, marked 'Most complete', button 'Get All Apps + Training'). A package button opens Stripe Checkout in a new tab; the page notes that your purchase is verified server-side before access is granted.
- If you already own 'DIY App Builder' and want the training, click 'Upgrade to Apps + Training for $400' under the cards. The studio then shows 'Redirecting to secure checkout…'. If you already have the training it says 'You already have the Apps + Training package, so there is nothing to upgrade.'; if the upgrade does not apply to your account it explains that it is only for owners of the DIY App Builder package.

chunks.title: SmartVideo GO AI Apps — How to use
chunks.text:
SmartVideo GO AI Apps (/studio/apps). How to use.
- Scroll to 'How It Works' for the three steps: 'Choose Your App', 'Customize & Build' and 'Launch Your Business'. Under them, click 'Reseller Setup Walkthrough' to open the guided course at /academy/reseller/launch. The course page asks you to sign in and is available to accounts with the Apps + Training package; other accounts see a locked panel.
- To browse the collection, go to 'The Application Collection'. Type in the box 'Search SmartVideo GO AI Apps...' to search app names, descriptions and categories (the list updates after a short pause), and click a category button to filter: All, Image, Video, Business, Productivity, Audio, Creative, Real Estate, Design, Lifestyle or Marketing. A line such as 'Showing 12 of 38 applications' shows how many apps match. If nothing matches you see 'No apps found matching your criteria.'.
- Look at an app card: it shows a preview picture, the category, the name and a short description. Click the preview picture (or 'Try Live Demo') to open the working demo in a new tab. Cards without a hosted demo have no 'Try Live Demo' button.
- Click 'Deployment Guide' on a card to open that app's instructions in the Reseller Deployment Center (/reseller/deployment, jumping to the app's section).

chunks.title: SmartVideo GO AI Apps — How to use
chunks.text:
SmartVideo GO AI Apps (/studio/apps). How to use.
- Click 'Source Code' to open the app's GitHub repository in a new tab. If an app has no published repository the button is greyed out and its tooltip reads 'Repository not yet published'. A small 'GitHub' link at the bottom of the card goes to the same repository.
- Click 'Deploy on Vercel' to start importing the app's repository into your own Vercel account in a new tab. Only apps that are published as deployable templates have this button active; on the others it is greyed out and the tooltip reads 'Deploy unavailable — this app's source repository is not published as a deployable template.'
- Click 'Learn How to Launch This App' to open that app's guided launch workshop in the Reseller Academy (/academy/reseller/apps/<app id>). Like the walkthrough, it needs you to be signed in and to have the training access.
- For a complete beginner-to-launch route, follow 'Reseller Setup Walkthrough' (/academy/reseller/launch) alongside the 'Deployment Guide' of the app you picked.
gettingStarted:
- Open /studio/apps.
- Search or pick a category to find an app.
- Click 'Try Live Demo' to see it working.
- Click 'Deployment Guide' for the setup instructions and 'Source Code' for the repository.
- Click 'Reseller Setup Walkthrough' for the guided course.
tips:

chunks.title: Edit — Overview
chunks.text:
Edit (/studio/edit). Overview.
description: A gallery of 14 one-purpose AI tool cards (image and video generators, upscaler, background remover, watermark remover, face swap, product shot, lip sync, editors, motion controls, audio, anime). Each card opens its own playground.
shortDescription: A gallery of 14 one-purpose AI tool cards (image and video generators, upscaler, background remover, watermark remover, face swap, product shot, lip sync, editors, motion controls, audio, anime). Each card opens its own playground.
fullDescription: Edit Studio opens on a gallery of tool cards titled "AI tools, one click away". Each card is a standalone tool: click it to open a playground at /studio/edit/<tool-name> with only the upload boxes, prompt box and settings that the selected model needs. You can filter the gallery by All, Image, Video or Audio, switch tools from a dropdown without going back, run several generations in one session, download each result and send a result back in as the next input. Which upload boxes and settings appear depends on the model you pick in the Model dropdown.
bestFor: Creators who want single-purpose AI tools with minimal setup.
whenToUse:
- You want one specific job done fast (cut-out, upscale, watermark removal, face swap, lip sync)
- You want a simple playground with only the needed inputs
whenToUseAnother:

chunks.title: Edit — Overview
chunks.text:
Edit (/studio/edit). Overview.
- Use Image Studio for a full prompt bar with history and many image models
- Use Video Studio for the full video workflow with modes and per-model controls
- Use Layers Studio for layer decomposition, canvas expansion and color grading
businessValue: One place to run common AI edit jobs without learning a full studio.

chunks.title: Edit — How to use
chunks.text:
Edit (/studio/edit). How to use.
howToUse: Open the Edit tab in the studio tab bar, or go to /studio/edit. You will see the gallery headed "AI tools, one click away". Optionally click All, Image, Video or Audio above the cards to show only that kind of tool. Click the card for the tool you want (for example Background Remover). Each card shows its name, a one-line hint and the number of models it offers.
howToSteps:
- Open the Edit tab in the studio tab bar, or go to /studio/edit. You will see the gallery headed "AI tools, one click away".
- Optionally click All, Image, Video or Audio above the cards to show only that kind of tool.
- Click the card for the tool you want (for example Background Remover). Each card shows its name, a one-line hint and the number of models it offers.
- In the playground, if the Model dropdown is shown, choose a model. Each model has its own upload boxes and settings.
- Add the required inputs. Boxes marked with an asterisk (*) are required; boxes marked (optional) can be skipped. For each box, click it or drop a file on it, or paste a link under "or paste an image URL" (the word changes to video or audio for those boxes) and click Add, or click Saved to pick a file you uploaded or generated earlier.
- If a Prompt box is shown, type what you want. A Prompt marked with * is required; the placeholder text tells you what to write.

chunks.title: Edit — How to use
chunks.text:
Edit (/studio/edit). How to use.
- If a Settings panel is shown, adjust the options. Changing the model resets Settings to that model's defaults.
- Click Generate. While it runs, the Result panel shows "Generating…" with a seconds counter and the button reads Run again.
- When the result appears, click Download to save it, or Use as input to send it into the first matching upload box of the same tool for another pass.
- To compare runs, use the This session strip (it appears after the second run) and click a thumbnail. Use ← All tools to go back to the gallery, or Switch tool to open a different one.
gettingStarted:
- Open the Edit tab (route /studio/edit).
- Click a tool card, for example Image Upscale.
- Upload your file in the box marked with *, or paste its URL and click Add.
- Pick a model in the Model dropdown if one is shown, and fill in the Prompt if one is shown.
- Click Generate, wait for the result, then click Download.
tips:
- Start from the card whose name matches your goal: the tool already limits the Model list to models that fit it.
- Use Use as input to chain steps, for example generate with AI Image Generator, then open Image Upscale and add the result with Saved or Use as input.
- Bookmark /studio/edit/<tool-name> to jump straight into a tool; the browser Back button returns to the gallery.
- Check the short description under the Model dropdown: it describes the selected model.

chunks.title: Edit — How to use
chunks.text:
Edit (/studio/edit). How to use.
- Uploads are checked by file type: an image box rejects non-image files with a message.
bestPractices:
- Read which boxes are marked * before you click Generate; a missing required file or Prompt shows a message and nothing runs.
- Wait for "Uploading…" to finish before clicking Generate; the button is disabled while an upload is running.
- Keep one tool open per task and use the This session strip to compare variations instead of re-uploading.
- Use clear, direct prompts that match the placeholder shown in the Prompt box.

troubleshooting:
- Nothing happens when I click Generate / error message appears: Read the message in the corner or in the Result panel; it names what is missing, for example 'Please enter a prompt.' or 'Please add: source video.'

- Generate button is greyed out: An upload is still in progress ('Uploading… N%'). Wait for it to finish.
- Thumbnail on a card is missing: Cards show a gradient with an icon when the thumbnail cannot load. The tool still works; click the card.
troubleshootingSteps:

- issue: Upload fails or is rejected | steps:; - Make sure the file type matches the box (image, video or audio).; - For a link, paste the full address starting with http:// or https:// and click Add.; - Try again, or pick the file with Saved.

chunks.title: Motion Control — Overview
chunks.text:
Motion Control (/studio/motion-control). Overview.
description: Upload a reference video and one or more character images, and the studio rebuilds the video with your characters while keeping the original motion (Motion Transfer), or swaps outfits, characters or products in the same scene (Objects Swap).
shortDescription: Upload a reference video and one or more character images, and the studio rebuilds the video with your characters while keeping the original motion (Motion Transfer), or swaps outfits, characters or products in the same scene (Objects Swap).
fullDescription: Motion Control uses Seedance Motion Control models. You supply a reference video that holds the movement, choreography and camera work you want, plus one or more character or performer images. In Motion Transfer mode the studio extracts the motion from the video and rebuilds the scene with your characters. In Objects Swap mode the video scene is kept unchanged while outfits, characters or products are swapped for those in your images. An optional text box adds extra scene, lighting or motion notes. You choose the model, aspect ratio, duration, audio and advanced options in the bottom bar and click Generate Motion. Finished videos are shown in a gallery that is kept in your browser.
bestFor: Creators and marketers who want to reuse a recorded movement with their own character or product.
whenToUse:

chunks.title: Motion Control — Overview
chunks.text:
Motion Control (/studio/motion-control). Overview.
- You have a video with the movement you want and images of the character to use
- You want to swap outfits, characters or products in an existing video
whenToUseAnother:
- Use Video Studio to create video from a text prompt or a single image
- Use Vibe Motion for animated graphics from text
- Use Lip Sync studio to make a face speak audio
businessValue: Motion Control reuses real motion with new characters or products so you can make variations without re-filming.

chunks.title: Motion Control — How to use
chunks.text:
Motion Control (/studio/motion-control). How to use.
howToUse: Open Motion Control at /studio/motion-control, choose Motion Transfer or Objects Swap, upload a reference video and at least one character image, optionally add a short instruction, adjust the model, aspect ratio, duration and options, then click Generate Motion.
howToSteps:
- Open Motion Control: choose Motion Control in the studio list, or go to /studio/motion-control.
- At the top of the bottom bar choose Motion Transfer (rebuild the scene with your character using the video motion) or Objects Swap (keep the scene and swap outfits, characters or products).
- Add the reference video: click the video button at the left (tooltip Upload reference video (MP4/WebM/MOV) or drag and drop) and pick a file up to 100 MB, or drag a video onto it, or click Library or Saved and choose a video. A preview shows when it is ready.
- Add at least one character image: click the image button (tooltip Upload character or performer images (PNG/JPEG/WebP)) and choose one or more images up to 20 MB each, or pick images from Library (Add as Image) or Saved. Click the + button to add more; click the x on a thumbnail (tooltip Remove image) to remove one.
- Optional: type extra scene, lighting or motion notes in the text box (the placeholder starts with Optional — describe additional scene details).

chunks.title: Motion Control — How to use
chunks.text:
Motion Control (/studio/motion-control). How to use.
- Optional: click the model button (Seedance 2.5 by default) and choose a model from the Model menu. Remember the 2.0 model allows at most 9 images and 15 seconds.
- Click the aspect ratio button (16:9 by default) and choose from the Aspect Ratio menu. Click the duration button (5s by default) and drag the slider (starts at 4 seconds) or click a preset such as 10s.
- Optional: click Generate Audio to turn sound generation on. Click the sliders icon to set High Bitrate, Quality or Seed.
- Click Generate Motion. The button shows Generating... while the video is made.
- When it finishes, a new card appears in the gallery. Hover over it to preview, click it to watch fullscreen, and use the download button (tooltip Download) to save it. Use Use as Video on the card to make it the next reference video.
gettingStarted:
- Open Motion Control from the studio list (/studio/motion-control).
- Leave the mode on Motion Transfer for your first try.
- Upload a short reference video (under 100 MB) and one clear character image.
- Keep the default model, 16:9 and 5s.
- Click Generate Motion and wait for Generating... to finish.
- Preview and Download the result from the gallery.
tips:
- Use a clear image of your character; add more images if the model should see other angles or items (up to the model limit).
- Start with 5s and a short reference video before running long ones.

chunks.title: Motion Control — How to use
chunks.text:
Motion Control (/studio/motion-control). How to use.
- Use Objects Swap when the scene should stay exactly as filmed.
- Use the Seed box to try repeating a good result; leave -1 for random.
- Download results you want to keep: the gallery is stored in this browser.
bestPractices:
- Pick the model first, then set images and duration within its limits.
- Match the duration to the length of the movement you want copied.
- Keep the text box short; the studio already adds an instruction for the chosen mode.
- Use Library or Saved to reuse assets instead of uploading again.

chunks.title: Motion Control — Features
chunks.text:
Motion Control (/studio/motion-control). Features.
keyFeatures:
- Two modes: Motion Transfer and Objects Swap
- Reference video upload (up to 100 MB; MP4, WebM or MOV) plus several character or performer images (up to 20 MB each)
- Model selector with several Seedance Motion Control models; the maximum duration and number of images depend on the chosen model
- Aspect ratio choice that depends on the model, default 16:9
- Duration slider starting at 4 seconds with quick presets (5s, 10s, 15s, 20s, 30s up to the model maximum), default 5s
- Generate Audio toggle, High Bitrate (2.5 models), Quality (2.0 model) and Seed options
- Library of your earlier videos, images and results, plus Saved (your shared library)
- Gallery of results with download, post, reuse as reference video and delete
featureExplanations:
- feature: Motion Transfer | explanation: Your character images take over the movement and camera work of the reference video. | whyToUse: Reuse a performance or choreography with a different character. | inputRequired: reference video and at least one character image | restrictions: Limits depend on the model.
- feature: Objects Swap | explanation: The reference scene stays as filmed while characters, outfits or products are replaced from your images. | whyToUse: Swap a product or outfit without re-shooting. | inputRequired: reference video and at least one image | restrictions: Limits depend on the model.

chunks.title: Motion Control — Features

chunks.title: Motion Control — Features
chunks.text:
Motion Control (/studio/motion-control). Features.
modelExplanations: Pick a model from the Model menu. The menu shows each model name with the start of its description. The default is Seedance 2.5 Motion Control. Seedance 2.0 Motion Control has a lower limit of 15 seconds and 9 images and offers a High or Basic Quality choice; the 2.5 models allow up to 30 seconds and 30 images and offer a High Bitrate switch. Other 2.5 variants listed in the menu follow the same limits; read their descriptions in the menu for what makes them different.

troubleshooting:
- Video or image upload fails
- Generation failed
- Generate Motion shows a missing video or image message
troubleshootingSteps:
- issue: Video or image upload fails | steps:; - Check the video is under 100 MB and each image under 20 MB (the messages are Video exceeds 100MB limit. and Image exceeds 20MB limit.).; - Try again; an error message shows the reason.; - Use MP4, WebM or MOV for video and PNG, JPEG or WebP for images.
- issue: Generation failed | steps:; - Read the error message at the top right.; - If generation is blocked, open the API keys settings and check your MuAPI key.; - Try a shorter duration, fewer images, or a different model, then click Generate Motion again.
- issue: Generate Motion shows a missing video or image message | steps:; - Load a reference video (the video button should show a preview).; - Add at least one character image (a count appears on the image button).; - Click Generate Motion again.
commonProblems:
- problem: A message says Please upload or select a reference video first. | whyItHappens: No reference video is loaded. | howToFix: Upload a video or choose one from Library or Saved.
- problem: A message says Please upload or select at least one character/performer image. | whyItHappens: No character image has been added. | howToFix: Add at least one image with the image button, Library or Saved.

Motion Control (/studio/motion-control). Problems and limits.
- problem: Maximum images message appears | whyItHappens: You reached the image limit of the selected model (9 for Seedance 2.0 Motion Control, 30 for the 2.5 models). | howToFix: Remove an image or switch to a model with a higher limit.
- problem: My duration or aspect ratio changed after switching model | whyItHappens: The new model does not support the old value, so the studio picked a supported one. | howToFix: Set the duration and aspect ratio again after choosing the model.
- problem: High Bitrate or Quality is not in the options popover | whyItHappens: High Bitrate shows only for the 2.5 models and Quality only for Seedance 2.0 Motion Control. | howToFix: Choose the model that has the option.
limitations:
- Reference video limited to 100 MB
- Each image limited to 20 MB
- Image count and duration depend on the model
- Minimum duration is 4 seconds
- Library and gallery are kept in this browser
limitationDetails:
- limitation: Reference video limited to 100 MB | impact: Larger files are refused. | workaround: Trim or compress the video.
- limitation: Each image limited to 20 MB | impact: Larger images are refused. | workaround: Resize or compress the image.
- limitation: Image count and duration depend on the model | impact: Seedance 2.0 Motion Control: 9 images and 15 seconds. 2.5 models: 30 images and 30 seconds. | workaround: Choose the model that fits.

chunks.title: Motion Control — Problems and limits
chunks.text:
Motion Control (/studio/motion-control). Problems and limits.
- limitation: Minimum duration is 4 seconds | impact: The slider starts at 4. | workaround: Trim the result afterwards if you need shorter.
- limitation: Library and gallery are kept in this browser | impact: They do not follow you to another browser. | workaround: Download results; use Saved for assets shared across studios.
faqs:
- question: Where do I open Motion Control? | answer: Choose Motion Control in the studio list, or go to /studio/motion-control.
- question: What is the difference between Motion Transfer and Objects Swap? | answer: Motion Transfer rebuilds the scene with your character using the motion of the video. Objects Swap keeps the video scene unchanged and swaps outfits, characters or products.
- question: What do I need before I can generate? | answer: A reference video and at least one character image. Without them you get messages asking you to add them.
- question: What are the file size limits? | answer: The reference video can be up to 100 MB and each image up to 20 MB.
- question: How many images and how many seconds can I use? | answer: It depends on the model: Seedance 2.0 Motion Control allows up to 9 images and 15 seconds; the 2.5 models allow up to 30 images and 30 seconds. The shortest duration is 4 seconds.
- question: Is the text box required? | answer: No. It is optional; the studio already adds an instruction for the selected mode.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — Overview
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). Overview.
description: A step-by-step builder for a vertical (9:16) animated explainer short: start from a topic, edit a starter script, generate character sheets and keyframe images, animate them into clips, add narration and optional music, then render the final video in your browser.
shortDescription: A step-by-step builder for a vertical (9:16) animated explainer short: start from a topic, edit a starter script, generate character sheets and keyframe images, animate them into clips, add narration and optional music, then render the final video in your browser.
fullDescription: Zack D Studio guides you through six numbered steps: Topic, Script, Characters & keyframes, Motion clips, Voice & music and Final cut. You start with one topic (or a template). The studio writes a fixed starter script of three beats that you edit by hand. After you approve the script, you pick a look, generate character sheets and one keyframe image per shot, animate each keyframe into a clip, generate narration (and optionally music), and finally render a 720x1280 video in your browser with transitions between shots. You can download the video or an .srt caption file, post it to social media, or pay to burn animated captions into it. Every paid generation asks for confirmation first, and your project is saved in this browser. The studio is adapted from the open-source Zack D Films project.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — Overview
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). Overview.
bestFor: Creators building short-form animated explainers who want control at each stage.
whenToUse:
- You want a complete vertical animated short built step by step from a topic
- You want to review and approve each stage before paying for the next
whenToUseAnother:
- Use Storyboard Studio to plan scenes more freely
- Use Video Studio for single generated clips
- Use Vibe Motion for animated graphics
businessValue: Zack D Studio puts script, images, clips, voice and final render in one guided flow, with confirmation before each paid step.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — How to use
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). How to use.
howToUse: Open Zack D Studio at /studio/zackd. Type a topic and click Write starter script (or load a template), edit the script and click Approve script, then work through the steps: generate character sheets and keyframes, approve keyframes, generate clips, generate narration, and render the video in Final cut.
howToSteps:
- Open Zack D Studio: choose Zack D Studio in the studio list, or go to /studio/zackd. Six step buttons (1. Topic to 6. Final cut) show where you are.
- On the Topic step, type a question or idea in the TOPIC field (up to 200 characters), or click one of the example topic cards to fill it in. To start from a template instead, scroll to Templates and click Use as template (finished demo) or Use script.
- Click Write starter script (it reads Rewrite starter script if a script already exists, and Continue current project takes you back to it). This builds a fixed three-beat script from your topic. No paid generation happens yet.
- On the Script step, read the beats and edit the narration box of each beat and the scene box of each shot to fit your idea. When it reads right, click Approve script.
- On the Characters & keyframes step, pick a look: Plasticine clay, Translucent glass or Bright toy studio.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — How to use
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). How to use.
- In Character sheets, click Generate all character sheet(s) and confirm the prompt, or use Generate on each card. Then in Keyframes click Generate all keyframe(s) and confirm. These are paid image calls on your MuAPI key. If a card looks wrong, click Redo on it.
- When every keyframe is done, click Approve keyframes to go to Motion clips.
- On Motion clips click Generate all clip(s) and confirm the prompt (the most expensive step; each clip takes a few minutes). Use Redo on any single clip you do not like. When all clips exist, click Continue to audio.
- On Voice & music choose a voice in the Voice dropdown, then click Generate narration (Regenerate narration if you already have one) and confirm. Optionally click Generate music under Background music (optional). Click Continue to final cut.
- On Final cut leave Keep the clips' own sound (Veo audio), quieter under narration on or off as you prefer, then click Render video. Wait while it shows Rendering and a percentage; click Cancel to stop.
- When the video appears, click Download video to save it. Optionally click Captions (.srt) for a free caption file, Post to social to publish it, or use Burn captions into the video (pick a Caption language and theme, then click Burn captions; the button reads Burn again once a captioned copy exists) for paid animated captions.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — How to use
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). How to use.
- To start over click New project and confirm. Your current project is saved in this browser until you do.
gettingStarted:
- Open Zack D Studio from the studio list (/studio/zackd).
- To try it with no paid generation, click Use as template on Swallow gum: finished demo in the Templates section.
- On the Script step, edit any text and click Approve script, then step through Approve keyframes and Continue to audio (a finished demo already has its keyframes and clips).
- On Final cut click Render video and then Download video.
- To make your own, start from a topic with Write starter script and follow the steps; every paid step asks for confirmation first.
tips:
- Edit the starter script: it is a generic skeleton built from your topic.
- Generate one item first (Generate on a single card) to check the look before running a whole batch.
- Pick the look before generating images; changing it later does not redo existing images.
- Use Redo only on the items that need it.
- The .srt file is free; burned-in captions cost extra.
- Use Chrome or Edge if your Post button says Post (needs MP4).
bestPractices:
- Finish and approve the script before spending on images.
- Check keyframes before generating clips, because clips are the most expensive step.
- Generate narration before rendering if you want narration in the video.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — How to use
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). How to use.
- Download the final video right after rendering: the rendered video is not kept if you leave or refresh the page, although the rest of the project is saved.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — Features
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). Features.
keyFeatures:
- Six-step guided flow with numbered step buttons: Topic, Script, Characters & keyframes, Motion clips, Voice & music, Final cut
- Starter script from your topic that you edit by hand (narration and scene text for each beat and shot)
- Templates: one finished demo and two script-only templates that need no paid generation to load
- Three looks: Plasticine clay, Translucent glass, Bright toy studio
- Character sheets and 9:16 keyframes generated as images; keyframes animated into clips
- Narration with a choice of preset voices, and optional background music
- Final cut rendered in your browser, with the option to keep the clips' own sound
- Downloads: video, free .srt captions file; paid burned-in animated captions; post to social
- Confirmation prompt before paid steps and a Redo button to retry any item
featureExplanations:
- feature: Starter script | explanation: Builds a three-beat script from your topic with a hook, a reaction beat and a resolution beat. The Script step then shows a count of beats and shots and the approximate length. | whyToUse: Gives you a structure to edit. | inputRequired: topic | restrictions: It is a generic skeleton, not an AI-written script. You edit the text.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — Features
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). Features.
- feature: Templates | explanation: Three templates: Swallow gum: finished demo (Use as template), Swallow gum: script only (Use script) and Mosquito bite: script only (Use script). | whyToUse: See a full example or reuse a ready script. | inputRequired: none | restrictions: Loading asks to confirm if you already have a script. Your chosen look and voice are kept.
- feature: Character sheets and keyframes | explanation: Generate all character sheet(s) and keyframe(s) in batches (up to three at a time), or one at a time with Generate or Redo on each card. | whyToUse: Get the images that will be animated. | inputRequired: approved script | restrictions: Each image is a paid call on your MuAPI key; a confirmation asks first for the batch buttons.
- feature: Motion clips | explanation: Animates each keyframe into a clip. | whyToUse: Turn still images into video. | inputRequired: all keyframes | restrictions: The batch button is disabled until every keyframe exists. Most expensive step.
- feature: Voice & music | explanation: Generates narration from all beat narration text, and optional background music. | whyToUse: Add sound. | inputRequired: script | restrictions: Music is optional.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — Features
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). Features.
- feature: Final cut | explanation: Renders in your browser at 720x1280: transitions between shots, impact zooms on marked shots, narration with music ducked underneath. Can take a minute or two. | whyToUse: Get the finished short. | inputRequired: a clip for every shot | restrictions: Needs a browser that can encode video; a Cancel button stops a render in progress.
- feature: Captions | explanation: Captions (.srt) downloads a free caption file. Burn captions into the video uploads your cut and adds animated word-by-word captions for a fee. | whyToUse: Subtitles or viral-style captions. | inputRequired: a rendered video; narration for burned-in captions | restrictions: Burned-in captions: about $0.20 minimum ($0.005 per second), 2-3 minutes.
advancedFeatures:
- Redo and per-item Generate
- Keep the clips' own sound
- Burn captions into the video
advancedFeatureExplanations:
- feature: Redo and per-item Generate | explanation: Each character sheet, keyframe and clip card has its own Generate or Redo button. | useCase: Fixing one item without regenerating everything | restrictions: Disabled while another job is running or without a key
- feature: Keep the clips' own sound | explanation: Mixes the Veo clip audio quietly under the narration. | useCase: Natural ambient sound | restrictions: none

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — Features
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). Features.
- feature: Burn captions into the video | explanation: Paid animated captions with a chosen language and theme. | useCase: Viral-style captions | restrictions: Needs narration
generationModes:
- Start from a topic
- Start from a template
modeExplanations:
- mode: Start from a topic | description: Type a topic and click Write starter script. The studio builds a fixed three-beat script skeleton from your topic; it does not write a custom script, so edit it. | acronymExpanded: N/A | useCase: Making your own short
- mode: Start from a template | description: Use as template loads the finished demo with its keyframes and clips; Use script loads only the script. Loading a template never calls a paid service. | acronymExpanded: N/A | useCase: Trying the studio at no cost or starting from a ready script
modelCapabilities: The studio uses MuAPI models behind the scenes: nano-banana-2 for images (with flux-dev-image as a fallback), Veo 3.1 fast image-to-video for clips (with the standard Veo 3.1 image-to-video as a fallback), a MiniMax speech model for narration, Suno for music and an AI captions service for burned-in captions. There is no model selector; the only choices on screen are the look, the voice and the caption language and theme.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — Features
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). Features.
modelExplanations: You do not choose models. If the first image or clip model fails or returns a placeholder, the studio tries the fallback automatically. The clips step text states that clips are animated with Veo 3.1 (fast, with the standard model as fallback), take a few minutes each and are the most expensive step. Narration uses preset MiniMax voices at a fixed speed. Music is optional.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — Problems and limits
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). Problems and limits.
troubleshooting:
- Images, clips or audio fail
- Render video fails or says the browser cannot encode video
- Project is not what I expected after loading a template
troubleshootingSteps:
- issue: Images, clips or audio fail | steps:; - Read the red message at the top of the studio; it says how many items failed.; - If generation is blocked, open the API keys settings and check your MuAPI key.; - Click Redo on the failed items.
- issue: Render video fails or says the browser cannot encode video | steps:; - Read the red message.; - Try again in Chrome or Edge.; - Make sure every shot has a clip.
- issue: Project is not what I expected after loading a template | steps:; - Loading a template replaces the current script and media (it asks Replace the current project with this template?).; - Your look and voice choices are kept.; - Click New project to start clean.
commonProblems:
- problem: Generate buttons are disabled | whyItHappens: No MuAPI key is set, or another job is running. | howToFix: Wait for the running job to finish. If generation is blocked, open the API keys settings and check your MuAPI key.
- problem: Generate all clip(s) is disabled | whyItHappens: Not every keyframe has been generated yet. | howToFix: Go back to Characters & keyframes and generate the missing keyframes.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — Problems and limits
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). Problems and limits.
- problem: Approve keyframes is disabled | whyItHappens: At least one keyframe is missing. | howToFix: Generate all keyframe(s) or click Generate on the missing cards.
- problem: A message says some items failed | whyItHappens: One or more jobs in the batch failed. | howToFix: Read the message, which ends with Use Redo to retry them., then click Redo on the failed items.
- problem: A message says shots have no clip yet | whyItHappens: Render video was clicked before every shot had a clip. | howToFix: Go to Motion clips and generate the missing clips.
- problem: Burn captions is disabled | whyItHappens: No narration has been generated, or no video has been rendered. | howToFix: Generate narration on Voice & music, render again, then click Burn captions.
- problem: Post to social reads Post (needs MP4) | whyItHappens: Your browser rendered a WebM file, which Instagram and TikTok reject. | howToFix: Render again in a browser that can make MP4, such as Chrome or Edge.
limitations:
- The starter script is a fixed skeleton
- Beats and shots cannot be added or removed in the screen
- Paid steps use your MuAPI credits
- The rendered video is not saved across page loads
- Voice cloning is not supported
- The final video is 9:16 only
limitationDetails:

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — Problems and limits
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). Problems and limits.
- limitation: The starter script is a fixed skeleton | impact: It does not write a custom script from your topic. | workaround: Edit the narration and scene text on the Script step.
- limitation: Beats and shots cannot be added or removed in the screen | impact: Only the text can be edited. | workaround: Rewrite the existing beats and shots.
- limitation: Paid steps use your MuAPI credits | impact: Character sheets, keyframes, clips, narration, music and burned-in captions each cost credits. | workaround: Use the confirmation prompts, generate one item first, and use the free templates to learn.
- limitation: The rendered video is not saved across page loads | impact: After a refresh you must click Render video again. | workaround: Download it right after rendering.
- limitation: Voice cloning is not supported | impact: Only preset voices can be chosen. | workaround: Pick the closest preset voice.
- limitation: The final video is 9:16 only | impact: The cut is rendered at 720x1280. | workaround: Re-edit elsewhere for other shapes.
faqs:
- question: Where do I open Zack D Studio? | answer: Choose Zack D Studio in the studio list, or go to /studio/zackd.
- question: Does it write the script for me? | answer: It builds a fixed three-beat starter script from your topic. It is a skeleton, so edit the narration and scene text on the Script step before you approve it.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — Problems and limits
chunks.text:
Zack D Studio (/studio/zackd). Problems and limits.
- question: What costs credits? | answer: Character sheets, keyframes, clips, narration, music and burned-in captions are paid calls on your MuAPI key. Loading a template and the free .srt file cost nothing. The studio asks you to confirm before each paid batch.
- question: How long does the final video render take? | answer: It renders in your browser and can take a minute or two. You can click Cancel to stop.
- question: What shape is the video? | answer: Vertical 9:16, rendered at 720x1280.
- question: Can I keep the sound from the generated clips? | answer: Yes. Keep the clips' own sound (Veo audio), quieter under narration is on by default in Final cut.
- question: Can I clone my voice? | answer: No. Only preset voices are offered.
- question: How much do burned-in captions cost? | answer: The studio says about $0.20 minimum ($0.005 per second) and 2-3 minutes. They need narration. The .srt file is free.
- question: Is my work saved? | answer: The project (script, images, clips, narration, music) is saved in this browser. The rendered video is not; download it after rendering.
- question: What is the difference between Use as template and Use script? | answer: Use as template loads the finished demo with its keyframes and clips. Use script loads just a script, and you generate the media yourself.

exampleWorkflows:
- title: Try it with the finished demo | steps:; - On Topic click Use as template under Swallow gum: finished demo.; - On Script click Approve script, then Approve keyframes and Continue to audio.; - On Voice & music click Continue to final cut.; - Click Render video, then Download video.
- title: Make your own short from a topic | steps:; - Type a topic and click Write starter script.; - Edit the narration and scene text, then click Approve script.; - Pick a look, generate character sheets and keyframes, then click Approve keyframes.; - Generate clips, generate narration, then render and download.
- title: Add burned-in captions | steps:; - Render the video on Final cut.; - Under Burn captions into the video pick a Caption language and a theme.; - Click Burn captions and confirm the price prompt.; - Click Open / download captioned video when it appears.

chunks.title: Zack D Studio — Glossary
chunks.text: Glossary: Beat: One unit of narration in the script, with one or more shots. | Shot: A single clip in the final video, with its own scene description. | Keyframe: The still 9:16 image that is animated into a clip. | Character sheet: A reference image of a recurring character or object. | Look: The visual style preset: Plasticine clay, Translucent glass or Bright toy studio. | Burned-in captions: Captions drawn into the video itself (paid), as opposed to the free .srt file.

Academy lesson: Screenplay & Story Generation.
# Screenplay & Story Generation
 SmartVideo GO AI Academy — Part of the SmartVideo GO AI course library. Everything in this lesson can be produced end-to-end inside SmartVideo GO AI using its Image, Video, Audio, Cinema, Lip-Sync, Storyboard, VFX, Thumbnail and AI Influencer studios, plus the Create-With-AI recipe system.
 A good script is cheap; a good story that can actually be filmed by AI is rare.
Track: AI Filmmaking
Time: ~40 minutes
Prerequisites: None

chunks.title: Screenplay & Story Generation — The Problem
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Screenplay & Story Generation / The Problem.
Traditional screenplays are written for human actors and camera crews. A standard script might describe "a crowded café with dozens of patrons chatting, as the protagonist slams their coffee cup down in anger, causing coffee to spill onto a passing waiter's uniform."
If you feed a scene like this into a generative AI video model, the rendering will fail completely. The patrons' faces will morph, the physical interaction of spilling coffee on a waiter will look like a surreal glitch, and keeping the protagonist looking like the same person across shots will be impossible.
Most aspiring AI filmmakers start by writing a standard story, only to waste hundreds of generation credits trying to force an AI model to render complex physics, crowds, or constant location shifts. Designing your screenplay with AI-first constraints from day one is the difference between a completed film and a folder of discarded, glitchy clips.

chunks.title: Screenplay & Story Generation — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Screenplay & Story Generation / The Concept.
AI-first screenwriting is the process of drafting stories designed specifically around the limitations and strengths of generative models.
### Core Constraints of Generative Video Models:
 The Physics Gap: AI models struggle with complex object interaction (e.g., tying shoes, pouring liquids, buttoning a shirt, eating food).
 The Crowd Dilemma: Any scene with more than two characters in frame dramatically increases visual morphing and reduces identity consistency.
 Continuous Action Limits: Most models generate clips in 4–5 second increments. Long, continuous single-take action scenes are not yet feasible.
To design around these constraints, we write scripts that focus on static character postures, environmental moods, atmospheric lighting, and high-impact dialogue/voiceover rather than complex physical action.
Story Outline → Constraint Check → Visual Script Formatting → Prompts Generation
Instead of describing physical struggle, describe the emotional reaction shown on a character's face or the mood of the setting, which AI video generators render beautifully.

chunks.title: Screenplay & Story Generation — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Screenplay & Story Generation / Do It.
### Step 1: Define the Production Constraints
Before writing a single word of your script, fill out the project constraints in your brief. Choose:
 Max 1–2 characters to maintain facial consistency.
 Max 2 locations (e.g., a quiet office, a dimly lit street).
 Atmospheric focus: Decide on the visual theme (e.g., neon cyberpunk, dusty retro-future, noir daylight) to anchor prompt styling.
### Step 2: Write the Screenplay with Visual Anchor Prompts
Format your screenplay using a layout that integrates standard screenwriting format with image/video prompt anchors.
 Break the script into individual, discrete shots (each lasting 3-4 seconds).
 For each shot, write a clear visual action description that details the character's facial expression or slow movement.
 Keep dialogue brief (under 15 words per shot) so that TTS models can read it naturally without rushing.
### Step 3: LLM Script Generation
Use a text LLM (like Claude or Gemini) to brainstorm and refine the script. Use a system prompt that forces the AI to respect physical limitations:

chunks.title: Screenplay & Story Generation — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Screenplay & Story Generation / Do It.
 System Prompt: "You are an AI-first screenwriter. Write a 60-second sci-fi script. Only 1 character. Set entirely in a single room. Avoid any physical object interactions. Focus on facial expressions, slow camera tracking shots, and voiceover dialogue. For every scene, output a detailed visual prompt describing camera movement, framing, character appearance, and lighting."
### Step 4: Prune the Actions
Review the script line by line. If a line says "He stands up, walks to the shelf, grabs a book, opens it, and smiles," prune it. Replace it with: "He sits at the desk, looking at the shelf. [Camera pushes in on his face, showing curiosity]." This is highly renderable.
### Step 5: Save Character & Style Anchors
Create a style sheet with your prompt prefixes (lighting, film stock, aspect ratio) so they can be copy-pasted into every image generator.

chunks.title: Storyboarding & Shot Planning
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Storyboarding & Shot Planning.
# Storyboarding & Shot Planning
 SmartVideo GO AI Academy — Part of the SmartVideo GO AI course library. Everything in this lesson can be produced end-to-end inside SmartVideo GO AI using its Image, Video, Audio, Cinema, Lip-Sync, Storyboard, VFX, Thumbnail and AI Influencer studios, plus the Create-With-AI recipe system.
 A storyboard is the blueprint that stops you from burning credits on random video generations.
Track: AI Filmmaking
Time: ~40 minutes
Prerequisites: Screenplay & Story Generation

chunks.title: Storyboarding & Shot Planning — The Problem
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Storyboarding & Shot Planning / The Problem.
Generating video clips directly from text prompts is a gamble. AI video models are expensive, slow to render, and highly unpredictable. If you type a prompt like "A spaceship interior, John walking towards the door" into a video generator, you might get a great shot, but John’s outfit might be blue, the room might be brightly lit, and the camera angle might be from the ceiling. If you run it again, John's face and clothes will change completely.
If you generate 20 video clips this way, you will end up with a collection of disjointed footage that looks like it belongs to 20 different movies. You will have wasted dozens of dollars in rendering credits and hours of waiting time.
To make a coherent film, you need to establish visual continuity — lighting, color palette, camera framing, and character wardrobe — before you render a single frame of video. Storyboarding is the gatekeeper that locks down these elements at a fraction of the cost.

chunks.title: Storyboarding & Shot Planning — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Storyboarding & Shot Planning / The Concept.
Storyboarding for AI filmmaking is the process of generating a sequence of static images that represent the key shots of your film.
By using high-quality image models (like Flux or Midjourney) instead of video models, you can rapidly test style, composition, and consistency. These static storyboard frames then act as the start-frame input for your image-to-video generator.
Visual Style Guide → Character Anchor → Storyboard Images → Image-to-Video
To maintain visual consistency across your storyboard, you rely on a Style Guide containing:
 Style Prefix: A standard set of visual descriptors (film stock, lighting, lens) added to every prompt.
 Aspect Ratio: Fixed layout matching your target screen format.
 Character Reference: A locked-in seed image of your character fed back into the model to maintain facial details.
---

chunks.title: Storyboarding & Shot Planning — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Storyboarding & Shot Planning / Do It.
### Step 1: Create the Visual Style Guide
Define your aesthetic parameters using the templates/style-guide-template.md. Lock in your film stock (e.g. 35mm film grain), your color palette (e.g. teal shadows, warm amber highlights), and your camera aspect ratio (e.g. --ar 16:9).
### Step 2: Establish the Character Anchor Image
Before drafting scenes, generate your character's "hero portrait."
 Write a detailed prompt describing the character's face, hair, age, and a specific wardrobe element (e.g., "A worn silver flight suit with a red shoulder patch").
 Generate this image using a high-quality model.
 Save the best image. This is your Character Reference Image (Cref).
### Step 3: Generate the Storyboard Frames
For each shot in your screenplay, generate the static frame.
 Start each prompt with your Style Prefix.
 Describe the framing (Wide Shot, Medium Shot, Close-up).
 Reference your Character Anchor Image using the model's image-to-image or character reference capabilities.
 Keep the scene seed constant if the model supports it, varying only the framing and character posture.
### Step 4: Build the Shot List
Log each generated frame into your templates/shot-list-template.md. Note the camera framing, target action, dialogue line, and the file path of the approved static storyboard image.
### Step 5: Check for Visual Continuity

chunks.title: Storyboarding & Shot Planning — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Storyboarding & Shot Planning / Do It.
Place the storyboard frames next to each other. Do a drift check:
 Does the character’s hair or outfit shift significantly between cuts?
 Does the environment’s lighting change color temperature?
 If yes, re-render the drifting frames, tightening the text prompts to override the changes.
---

Still no response from deep space relay Theta. If anyone is listening... this is my final transmission. The overhead monitor flickers aggressively before flashing stark green text: NO SIGNAL. ### Storyboard Shot List & Visual Examples #### Shot 1: Wide Establishing Shot (WS)

chunks.title: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts.
# Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts
 SmartVideo GO AI Academy — Part of the SmartVideo GO AI course library. Everything in this lesson can be produced end-to-end inside SmartVideo GO AI using its Image, Video, Audio, Cinema, Lip-Sync, Storyboard, VFX, Thumbnail and AI Influencer studios, plus the Create-With-AI recipe system.
 Camera movement is the difference between an AI slideshow and a movie.
Track: AI Filmmaking
Time: ~50 minutes
Prerequisites: Screenplay & Story Generation, Storyboarding & Shot Planning

chunks.title: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts — The Problem
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts / The Problem.
Most beginners in AI video generation end up creating what looks like a PowerPoint presentation with slight Ken Burns effects: static characters with wind blowing through their hair, or background dust drifting slightly.
If they try to force camera movements by typing generic text like "the camera moves fast," the video models often glitch, morphing the character's body parts or turning the entire background into a liquid smear.
Real cinema relies on deliberate, structured camera movements — dolly shots, pans, tilts, crane movements, and tracking shots. To make your AI film look premium and deliberate, you need to know how to prompt these movements in a way the video generator's neural network actually understands.

chunks.title: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts / The Concept.
Video models don't think like camera operators; they think in terms of pixel displacement and temporal flow. When you write a movement prompt, you are instructing the model on how pixels should slide across the screen from frame to frame.
To control this displacement effectively, you use three tools:
1. First-Frame Conditioning (Image-to-Video): You feed your storyboard frame from Module 2 as the starting point. This locks the framing and composition.
2. Cinematography Keywords: Using precise industry terms (dolly, pan, tilt) instead of vague action words.
3. Motion Strength Parameters: Adjusting the model's velocity settings to control how much the frame changes over time.
Start Frame (Storyboard) + Camera Direction Prompt + Motion Slider = Cinematic Shot
For advanced shots, you can use First and Last Frame Conditioning, uploading both the starting shot composition and the ending shot composition, forcing the model to generate the transition between them.
---

chunks.title: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts / Do It.
### Step 1: Prepare Your Storyboard Start-Frame
Select the static storyboard image you generated in Module 2. Make sure it is at your target aspect ratio (16:9 or 2.39:1). Upload it to your video generator's image-to-video input interface.
### Step 2: Formulate the Motion Prompt
Use the templates/motion-prompt-library.md to choose the camera movement that matches the shot's emotional goal. Add the camera movement phrase to the beginning of your prompt.
 Example: "Slow dolly in, camera slowly pushes toward the astronaut's face, Arri Alexa cinematic style, 24fps."
### Step 3: Set the Motion Strength Slider
If your generator supports it, adjust the motion strength value:
 For dialogue or subtle scenes: Set strength to Low (1–3). This prevents face warping while allowing subtle blinks and head tilts.
 For camera pans, walking, or panning b-roll: Set strength to Medium (4–6).
 For fast action, running, or driving: Set strength to High (7–9).
### Step 4: Render and Review
Render the 4-second clip. Watch the playback and check for:
 The Morphing Zone: Did the background objects bend? Did the character grow extra fingers or change clothes mid-shot?
 Pacing: Is the camera speed jarring or smooth?
 If the shot glitches, lower the motion strength slider and re-render. If it is too static, rewrite the prompt to place the camera direction at the very start of the text.

chunks.title: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts / Do It.
### Step 5: (Optional) Set Last-Frame Conditioning
If the action requires a precise end point, upload a second storyboard image to the Last-Frame Input box. Write a prompt describing the movement between the two images (e.g. "Camera pans left from the cockpit window to focus on the radar screen").

Track: AI Filmmaking
Time: ~50 minutes
Prerequisites: Screenplay & Story Generation, Storyboarding & Shot Planning, Camera Movement & Cinematography Prompts

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film — The Problem
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film / The Problem.
If you take raw, silent clips directly from a video generator and play them back-to-back, the result is jarring. One clip might have a slight green tint, the next is warm yellow. The camera motion speeds don't match. And most of all, the complete silence makes the video feel dead, revealing the artificial nature of the footage immediately.
Most tutorials focus purely on the generation phase, leaving you with a folder of silent, disconnected files.
An AI film only becomes a real movie when it enters the editor. You must stitch the clips together, establish narrative pacing, match the color palette across different generation runs, and build a rich, multi-layered audio track.

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film / The Concept.
Post-production assembly bridges the gap between silent AI clips and a finished cinematic piece. This workflow consists of two main pillars: Audio Layering and Color Grading.
### The Sound Design Hierarchy:
Because AI video clips are generated silent, you must build the audio track from scratch. We layer audio in a precise hierarchy:
1. Dialogue / Narration: The vocal performance (voiceover or synced speech).
2. Ambience / Room Tone: Continuous background noise that sets the space (e.g., spaceship engine hum, rain).
3. Foley / Sound Effects (SFX): Discrete sounds synchronized with visual events (e.g., switches clicking, heavy footsteps).
4. Music / Soundtrack: The emotional underscore of the scene.
Silent Visual Cuts → Narration → Ambience Track → Foley Sync → Music Score
### Visual Unification:
To fix slight shifts in color grading between different generations, you apply a LUT (Look-Up Table) to the entire editing timeline. This overlays a uniform color grade across all clips, blending them into a single visual style.
---

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film / Do It.
### Step 1: Organize Your Project Timeline
Import your generated clips into an NLE (Non-Linear Editor — a video editing program that lets you arrange and cut clips on a timeline) such as DaVinci Resolve, Premiere Pro, or CapCut. Lay them out in order on your main video track (V1). Trim any visual glitches that occur at the very beginning or end of a clip (video models often dissolve or warp in the final half-second).
### Step 2: Generate the Voiceover Narration
Use a high-quality TTS or voice-cloning API (like ElevenLabs).
 Paste your script from Module 1.
 Add artificial line breaks or punctuation (commas, ellipses) to force the voice model to pause naturally.
 Import the audio file into the editor on audio track A1. Sync the start of dialogue lines with your character's visual entrance.
### Step 3: Layer the Ambient Soundscape
Find or generate a continuous background noise track matching your film brief (e.g. static room tone or city rain). Place this on track A2. Fade it in at the opening frame and let it run continuously under all edits to unify the cuts.
### Step 4: Synchronize Foley SFX
Scroll through the video frame by frame. Wherever a physical action occurs (a screen flickers, a head turns, boots hit pavement), place a matching sound effect on track A3. Align the audio peak exactly with the visual moment of impact.
### Step 5: Score the Scene

chunks.title: Assembling a Short Film — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Assembling a Short Film / Do It.
Place your background music on track A4. Set the general music volume low (around -18dB to -24dB). Enable Audio Ducking so that the music automatically drops by an additional 6dB whenever the voice track (A1) is active.
### Step 6: Apply a Unified Color Grade
Select all video clips on V1. Add an adjustment layer over the entire timeline and apply a film emulation LUT (e.g. Kodak 2383 style). This unifies the highlights and shadow colors across all separate generations, hiding minor color discrepancies. Export the finished project at 24fps.
---

chunks.title: Selling Short-Form Films — The Problem
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Short-Form Films / The Problem.
Most people who make AI short films share them on YouTube or Twitter, get a few hundred views, and make $0. They treat it purely as a hobby or an art project. Because they don't understand the commercial market for digital media, they miss out on the growing economic ecosystem surrounding AI video production.
At the same time, brands are looking for cost-effective visual storytelling, new vertical drama platforms are spending millions of dollars licensing short episodes, and major technology companies are hosting AI film festivals with tens of thousands of dollars in cash prizes.
To turn AI filmmaking into a sustainable business, you must transition from "making cool clips" to understanding how to structure sponsorships, pitch licensing agreements, and target the right monetization funnels.

chunks.title: Selling Short-Form Films — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Selling Short-Form Films / The Concept.
Monetizing AI short-form video runs along three main avenues, each with a different financial return and effort level:
 ┌───────────────────────┐
 │ AI Film Festivals │ ──► Cash Prizes ($1K - $20K) & Brand Exposure
 ├───────────────────────┤
AI Short Film ──► │ Brand Sponsorships │ ──► Direct Product Placement ($300 - $1.5K)
 ├───────────────────────┤
 │ Platform Licensing │ ──► Ep. Sales to Vertical Apps ($150 - $500/ep)
 └───────────────────────┘
1. AI Film Festivals: High prestige, low predictability. Submitted through aggregator directories, these offer cash prizes and direct introductions to agency directors.
2. Brand Sponsorships: Moderate predictability, high margins. You integrate a brand's digital asset (a logo, a product model) into the world of your film.
3. Platform Licensing: Highest predictability, volume-driven. Vertical video platforms (ReelShort, DramaBox, etc.) buy rights to short-form episodic narrative content.

Use templates/sponsorship-pitch-template.md to outline your project's concept. Include your static storyboard frames from Module 2 to show the high visual quality of the project before it is rendered.
### Step 3: Pitch Brand Sponsorships
Search for mid-sized brands whose aesthetic matches your film theme.
 Example: If you are making a sci-fi film, target premium desk accessory or software companies. If you are making a drama, target fashion or skincare brands.
 Send your pitch offering seamless product integration inside your narrative world. Charge an upfront fee ($300–$1,000 for initial campaigns).
### Step 4: Submit to AI Film Festivals
Set up a profile on FilmFreeway. Search for "AI Film Festivals." Submissions are often free or low-cost. Submit to major ones (e.g. Runway AIFF, muapi Creator Awards) to build industry credibility.

chunks.title: Cinematography Cheat Sheet — 1. Camera Framing Terms
chunks.text:
Academy template: Cinematography Cheat Sheet / 1. Camera Framing Terms.
 Extreme Wide Shot (EWS): Environment is the subject; character is tiny or not visible.
 Wide Shot (WS): Full body of the character is visible; details of the location are clear.
 Medium Wide Shot (MWS): Knee-up framing.
 Medium Shot (MS): Waist-up framing.
 Close-up (CU): Chest/shoulders-up framing.

chunks.title: Sound Design Checklist — 1. Dialogue / Narration Layer
chunks.text:
Academy template: Sound Design Checklist / 1. Dialogue / Narration Layer.
- [ ] Clean Dialogue: Ensure the generated voice (TTS/Voice Clone) is free of digital artifacts or slurring.
- [ ] Room Tone: Add a very quiet ambient layer matching the environment under the dry voice clip so the speaker doesn't sound like they are in a vacuum.
- [ ] Pacing & Pauses: Add artificial pauses (0.5 to 1.5 seconds) between sentences. Real people breathe and pause; AI TTS often runs sentences together.

chunks.title: Sound Design Checklist — 2. Ambient Soundscape (Background)
chunks.text:
Academy template: Sound Design Checklist / 2. Ambient Soundscape (Background).
- [ ] Primary Environment Ambience: Layer continuous background sound matching the location (e.g., wind rustle for forest, low rumble for spaceship interior, city traffic chatter).
- [ ] Transitions: Fade ambience in/out during scene changes to smooth out cuts.

chunks.title: Sound Design Checklist — 3. Foley & Sound Effects (SFX)
chunks.text:
Academy template: Sound Design Checklist / 3. Foley & Sound Effects (SFX).
- [ ] Action Syncing: Add synchronized sound effects for physical actions shown on screen (e.g., doors opening, footsteps, coffee cups clinking, keyboard clicks).
- [ ] Audio Sweeps: Use riser or whoosh sounds to match rapid camera pans or transitions.

chunks.title: Sound Design Checklist — 4. Music & Score
chunks.text:
Academy template: Sound Design Checklist / 4. Music & Score.
- [ ] Tone Alignment: Match the music genre to the film's genre.
- [ ] Dynamic Level: Duck the music volume by 6dB to 12dB whenever dialogue is playing.
- [ ] Key Syncing: Sync visual cuts to the beat or transition points in the music track where possible.

chunks.title: Sound Design Checklist — 5. Master Output Check
chunks.text:
Academy template: Sound Design Checklist / 5. Master Output Check.
- [ ] Level Balance: Dialogue should be clearly audible, music secondary, SFX tertiary.
- [ ] No Clipping: Ensure the audio master meter never peaks into the red (above 0dB).

### 1. Niche Selection & Script Pipeline
 If your niche has low CPM, your view count doesn't matter; if your script has low retention, YouTube won't show it to anyone.
- Evaluate advertiser density and identify high-CPM niches (Finance, SaaS, Business).

Templates: niche-evaluation-matrix.md · retention-script-template.md
### 2. Duration-Matched Narration & Pacing
 Visuals tell the story, but the audio duration controls the edit.
- Lay down voice narration audio tracks first to establish the spine of your editing timeline.
- Measure and log exact audio clip durations to schedule visual cuts every 2–4 seconds.
- Trim trailing pauses and silent frames to maintain rapid, drop-free pacing.
Templates: narration-duration-log.md
### 3. Honest RPM & Earnings Math
 Views are vanity; profit margins are sanity.
- Demystify long-form vs. short-form AdSense payouts (Shorts RPM of $0.02-$0.06 vs. long-form RPM of $5-$25).
- Audit API generation costs (scripting, text-to-speech, video credits) to calculate unit costs per video.
- Design lead-generation conversion rates to make a small channel profitable from day one.
Templates: channel-profitability-calculator.md
### 4. Scaling to Multiple Channels
 One channel is a job; three channels is a system.
- Establish temporal batch schedules (scripting on Mondays, voiceovers on Tuesdays, rendering on Wednesdays).
- Run multiple channel accounts safely on a single computer using isolated browser profiles.
