|---|---|---|---|
| Batch Prompt Runner | Sends 50+ prompts to FLUX/muapi in one click | AI image creators | $29 – $49 |
| Etsy SEO Title Generator | Generates 3 title + keyword sets per product from a name list | POD sellers | $19 – $39 |
| Stock Metadata CSV Writer | Reads image filenames and writes 30 IPTC keywords per image | Stock contributors | $29 – $59 |
| Pricing Calculator Widget | Interactive web form that calculates package pricing for a client | Agency freelancers | $19 – $29 |

chunks.title: The Vibe-Coding Workflow: Prompt → Build → Test → Ship — The Problem
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Vibe-Coding Workflow: Prompt → Build → Test → Ship / The Problem.
Most creators who start vibe-coding hit the same wall after their second or third tool:
 The agent produces a file that crashes on the first run.
 The creator pastes the error message back, the agent fixes it, but now something else breaks.
 After 3 rounds of back-and-forth, the session devolves into confusion and the project is abandoned.
This happens because vibe-coding without a structured workflow is just random prompting. A disciplined 4-phase loop — Prompt → Build → Test → Ship — eliminates this failure pattern by giving both you and the agent a clear contract for what each phase produces.
---

chunks.title: The Vibe-Coding Workflow: Prompt → Build → Test → Ship — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Vibe-Coding Workflow: Prompt → Build → Test → Ship / The Concept.
The Vibe-Coding Loop is a repeatable session structure:
Phase 1: PROMPT (Define Scope) ──► Phase 2: BUILD (Agent Generates) ──► Phase 3: TEST (You Verify) ──► Phase 4: SHIP (Package & Publish)
### Phase Breakdown:
#### Phase 1 — PROMPT (10 minutes)
Write the Tool Spec Brief (see templates/vibe-coding-session-brief.md) before opening the agent. Your brief must include:
 One-sentence tool description (what it does, for whom, using what input/output).
 Error handling rules (e.g., "if a line in the input file is blank, skip it and continue").
 Tech constraints (e.g., "use only Python standard library — no external packages except openai").
 The Golden Rule of Prompting for Code: Never open the agent without a written brief. Improvised prompting produces improvised code that breaks unpredictably.
#### Phase 2 — BUILD (15–30 minutes)
Paste your full brief into the agent in a single message. Let the agent generate the complete initial version without interrupting. Then:
 Read the agent's explanation of what it built (not the code — the explanation in plain English).
 If the explanation matches your brief, proceed to Phase 3.
 If it doesn't match, correct the agent with a targeted single-sentence fix, not a full re-description.
#### Phase 3 — TEST (10–15 minutes)

chunks.title: The Vibe-Coding Workflow: Prompt → Build → Test → Ship — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: The Vibe-Coding Workflow: Prompt → Build → Test → Ship / The Concept.
Run the tool on real data — not dummy placeholder data. Use the actual filenames, actual product names, or actual prompts your buyers will use. Check:
 ✅ Does it produce the correct output format?
 ✅ Does it handle edge cases gracefully (blank lines, special characters, long strings)?
 ✅ Does it complete in under 60 seconds for a typical input size?
When you find a bug, paste the exact error message (not a paraphrase) back to the agent:
 "Running the script gives this error: KeyError: 'title1'. Fix it."
#### Phase 4 — SHIP (10 minutes)
Ask the agent to generate the packaging assets:
 "Write a plain-English README.md explaining installation and usage. Also create a requirements.txt listing all pip packages needed."
Zip the folder: [tool-name]-v1.0.zip. Upload to Gumroad or LemonSqueezy. Done.
---

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling Tools You Build With Agents — The Problem
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling Tools You Build With Agents / The Problem.
Most creators who build a working micro-tool undercharge or don't charge at all. They post the tool for free on GitHub, get 200 stars, and make $0.
Others price based on gut feel — $5 because "it's just a script" — without understanding that buyers are paying for time saved, not code complexity. A script that saves 10 hours per week is worth far more than $5 regardless of how simple it looks.
Meanwhile, the minority who price correctly and list on the right platforms discover that a single well-scoped tool can generate $500 to $3,000 in the first 30 days from a creator audience of a few thousand.
---

chunks.title: Pricing & Selling Tools You Build With Agents — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Pricing & Selling Tools You Build With Agents / The Concept.
The Creator Tool Monetization Stack sells through three channels simultaneously:
Micro-Tool ──► Direct Gumroad/LemonSqueezy Page ──► Creator Community Launch ──► Affiliate Partner Network ──► Passive Recurring Revenue
### The Tool Pricing Formula:
$$\text{Tool Price} = \text{Hours Saved Per Month} \times \text{Buyer's Hourly Rate} \times 0.10$$
 Plain English: Price your tool at roughly 10% of the monthly value it saves the buyer. If your tool saves an Etsy seller 8 hours/month of keyword research, and their time is worth $25/hour, the tool is saving them $200/month — so charge $20 one-time (or $9/month if it requires ongoing API costs).
### Pricing Model Options:
1. One-Time Lifetime License (Most Popular for Scripts): Single payment, buyer owns the tool forever. Best for Python scripts with no ongoing server costs. Converts at 3–5x the rate of subscriptions for audiences under 10,000 followers.
2. Monthly Subscription (Best for Tools with API Costs): If your tool calls GPT-4 or muapi on every run, pass your API costs to the buyer via a $9–$29/month subscription. Use LemonSqueezy for subscription billing.
3. Pay-What-You-Want with a Minimum: Set a floor of $9 with a suggested price of $25. Gumroad supports this natively and frequently generates higher average revenue than a fixed price.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe.
# Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe
 SmartVideo GO AI Academy — Take one of the ready-made reseller apps from your own GitHub copy to a live, hosted business, with an AI chat doing the technical work for you through connectors.
---

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Who this track is for
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Who this track is for.
You own (or are about to own) one of the 38 reseller apps and you are not a developer. You do not want to learn a framework. You want to be able to say "host this", "add sign-up", "check the payment went through" to a chat and have it done, while you stay in control of what changes and what it costs.
If you can create accounts, copy and paste, and read a screen carefully, you can do this track. Every step tells you what you should see when it worked.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — What you will build
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / What you will build.
By the end you will have, for one app of your choice:
1. Free accounts on Netlify, Clerk and Stripe (Stripe in test mode), alongside GitHub.
2. Connectors that let Claude and/or ChatGPT see and use those services with your approval.
3. Your app built and hosted on Netlify from your own GitHub copy, at a netlify.app address.
4. Clerk sign-up and sign-in so real people can create accounts.
5. Stripe test payments that add credits, which you can check by asking the chat.
6. A reusable set of prompts so the next app takes a fraction of the time.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — The lessons
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / The lessons.
Every lesson takes under 20 minutes, so you can finish one in a sitting and stop at a safe point.
| # | Lesson | Time | What you finish with |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Start your free accounts | 18 min | Netlify, Clerk, Stripe (test), GitHub |
| 2 | Connect Claude with connectors | 18 min | Claude can read your three services |
| 3 | Connect ChatGPT the same way | 15 min | ChatGPT can, or you know it cannot on your plan |
| 4 | Brief your assistant on the app | 18 min | An assistant that understands your app |
| 5 | Check readiness and create the Netlify site | 18 min | A Netlify site connected to your repo |
| 6 | Add variables, deploy and fix failures | 18 min | A live netlify.app address |
| 7 | Plan the Clerk change | 15 min | A reviewed plan that protects credits |
| 8 | Make the Clerk change and add the keys | 15 min | Clerk on a preview deploy |
| 9 | Test sign-up and merge | 15 min | Real sign-up and sign-in, merged |
| 10 | Stripe keys and the webhook | 18 min | Test keys and a webhook endpoint |
| 11 | Test purchase and check it from the chat | 15 min | A test purchase that adds credits |
| 12 | Save your prompts and run the customer test | 15 min | A repeatable checklist |
| 13 | Go live: domain, Clerk production, Stripe live | 18 min | A live business |
Plan on a weekend for your first app, taking breaks between lessons. The second app will take an afternoon.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — What the apps already include (and what they do not)
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / What the apps already include (and what they do not).
Be clear about this before you start, because it decides what your assistant has to change.
 Already in the apps: Stripe payments and credit packs, a PostgreSQL database accessed through Prisma, Google sign-in through NextAuth, and the AI calls through your own MuAPI key. Each app's workshop page lists its exact variable names.
 Not in the apps: Netlify hosting settings and Clerk sign-in. Your assistant adds those to your own copy of the code, on a separate branch, and you approve every step.
This is why the track is a build and not a button: you are making two real changes to a real application, safely.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — How this track fits with the Reseller Setup Walkthrough
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / How this track fits with the Reseller Setup Walkthrough.
The Reseller Setup Walkthrough (/academy/reseller/launch) takes you through Vercel-based deployment, the database, Google sign-in, Stripe and launch for the app you select. Module 13 of that course is the interactive version of this track: Learn, Follow along, Complete and Verify for each lesson, with your selected app's facts shown beside the steps. Use this track to understand the whole picture; use Module 13 to do the work.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — The rules that keep you safe
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / The rules that keep you safe.
 Sign in to your own accounts only. Never connect a client's or an employer's account to practise.
 Read-only first. Before a chat is allowed to change anything, test it with a question that only reads.
 Never paste a secret key into a chat. Not Stripe keys, not the Clerk secret key, not database addresses, not the MuAPI key. Secrets go into the dashboard settings of Netlify, Clerk and Stripe. The assistant's job is to tell you which variable name to fill in; your job is to paste the value into the dashboard yourself.
 Test mode until you decide otherwise. Stripe stays in test mode, and Clerk stays on its development instance, until lesson 8.
 Small steps, explained first. Ask the assistant to say what it will change and why before it changes it. You can undo anything in GitHub.
 Menus change. Claude, ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe all rename and move things. This track teaches the flow and tells you what the result should look like; when a label differs, follow the service's official page.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — How to use an assistant well (the habits that matter)
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / How to use an assistant well (the habits that matter).
1. Give context once, clearly (lesson 4), then refer back to it.
2. Ask for a plan before a change. "Plan how to... Do not change anything yet."
3. One change at a time. After each, test it before the next.
4. Make it show evidence. "Show me the file you changed." "Read the deploy log and tell me the first error."
5. Keep a note of what worked, because the prompts become your template for every later app.

chunks.title: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Words you will meet
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 16: Build and Launch Apps with Claude or ChatGPT, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Words you will meet.
 Repository (repo): your app's folder of code on GitHub.
 Branch: a separate line of changes you can test without touching the working app.
 Deploy: building the app and putting it online.
 Environment variable: a named setting (like a key) kept in the hosting dashboard, not in the code.
 Webhook: a message Stripe sends your app to say a payment happened.
 Connector (plugin): a switch that lets Claude or ChatGPT use another service for you.
 Test mode: Stripe's practice mode: fake cards, no real money.
When you are ready, start with lesson 1. Each lesson ends at a safe stopping point.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe.
# Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: GitHub, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe accounts, all protected, with Stripe in test mode.
---

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Why four accounts
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Why four accounts.
A live app is several services working together. Each account has one job, and knowing the job makes every later step make sense.
| Account | Its one job | What you will put in it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub | Stores your own copy of the app's code | The repository for your chosen app |
| Netlify | Builds the code and serves it on the internet | Your site and its environment variables |
| Clerk | Handles sign-up, sign-in and user accounts | Your application and its keys |
| Stripe | Takes payments and reports them | Test keys, a webhook, test payments |
The AI part (MuAPI) and the database (Supabase or Neon) you already set up in Modules 4 and 5 of the Reseller Setup Walkthrough. If you have not done those, finish them first; lesson 6 needs the database address.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — What "free" means here
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / What "free" means here.
All three services offer a free plan at the time of writing. That does not mean free forever at any size. Free plans have limits (for example on build minutes, bandwidth or monthly active users), and the numbers change. Before you rely on any of them:
1. Open each pricing page.
2. Find the current free plan.
3. Write the main limits in your own notes, with today's date.
A free plan is more than enough to build and test, and often to take your first customers. You decide later whether to upgrade; nothing in this track asks you to pay.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Step by step.
### 1. GitHub
Sign in to the account you used in the Reseller Setup Walkthrough. Your app should already be forked into your own account. If not, do that first, because Netlify deploys from your copy.
### 2. Netlify
1. Open Netlify's sign-up page.
2. Choose Sign up with GitHub. This lets Netlify read the repositories you choose, which makes lesson 5 easier.
3. When asked, accept the free plan and give your team a name matching your business.
4. You should land on your team dashboard (a list of projects, empty for now).
### 3. Clerk
1. Open Clerk's sign-up page and create an account.
2. Create an application. Name it after your business. This is the name people see on sign-up screens.
3. Choose the sign-in options: keep Email and Google. Add others later if you want.
4. Clerk creates a development instance for you. This is the practice version: it works on netlify.app and preview addresses, and it is where you stay until you have your own domain.
5. Find the API keys page. You will see a publishable key and a secret key. Do not copy them anywhere yet; just know where they are.
### 4. Stripe
1. Create or sign in to your Stripe account.
2. Make sure you are in test mode (Stripe shows a Test mode or Sandbox indicator in the dashboard). Everything in this track uses test mode.
3. You do not need to activate your account for real payments yet. That is lesson 13 and Module 9.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Step by step.
### 5. Protect every account
For each of the four accounts:
 Turn on two-step sign-in.
 Use a strong, unique password in a password manager.
 Use your business email, so the accounts do not depend on a personal address.
These accounts control your app, your customers' sign-ups and your payments. Treat them like the keys to a shop.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Check yourself.
 [ ] I can open GitHub, Netlify, Clerk and Stripe dashboards.
 [ ] Stripe shows test mode.
 [ ] Clerk shows a development instance.
 [ ] Two-step sign-in is on for all four.
 [ ] I wrote down each free plan's limits and the date.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Common mistakes.
 Skipping the pricing pages, then discovering a limit mid-launch.
 Using a personal email, which makes handing the business over harder later.
 Switching Stripe to live too early. There is nothing to gain before the test purchase works.
 Connecting a client's account to practise. Use your own.

chunks.title: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — If something is off
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Start your free accounts: Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / If something is off.
 Clerk asks me to choose a plan. Choose the free plan if the current pricing page offers one. If not, re-check the page before paying for anything.
 Netlify cannot see my repo. You can change which repositories Netlify may read in your GitHub settings under installed applications.
Next: lesson 2, connecting Claude.

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe.
# Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: Claude connected to your three services, proven by a read-only test.
---

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — What a connector is
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / What a connector is.
Without connectors, a chat can only talk. It can explain how to deploy a site, but it cannot see your Netlify account. A connector (sometimes called a plugin or an integration) gives the chat a controlled way to use another service as you. You sign in to the service, approve what the chat may do, and from then on you can say:
 "List my Netlify sites and their last deploy."
 "Show my five most recent Stripe test payments."
 "Which Clerk application am I connected to?"
Most connectors are built on an open standard called the Model Context Protocol (MCP). You do not need to understand it. What you do need to understand is the trust model:
1. You sign in to the real service.
2. The service tells you what the chat is asking permission to do.
3. You approve it, and you can remove it any time from the same settings.
The chat never needs your password or your secret keys, because the connector holds the sign-in.

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Which connectors
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Which connectors.
Netlify, Stripe and Clerk each offer a connector for Claude. Availability depends on your Claude plan and on whether your workspace allows connectors, and the names and places of the menus change. So this lesson teaches the flow and what the result looks like; where a label differs, follow the official page for each service.

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Step by step.
### 1. Open the connector settings
Open Claude, sign in, and open its settings. Look for the area that manages connectors (or integrations). If you cannot find it, your plan or workspace may restrict it; check the official help page for your plan, or ask your workspace admin.
### 2. Add Netlify
1. Add the Netlify connector.
2. A Netlify sign-in page opens. Sign in with the account from lesson 1.
3. Netlify shows what is being requested. Approve access for your own team only.
4. Back in Claude, Netlify shows as connected.
### 3. Add Stripe
1. Add the Stripe connector and sign in.
2. Choose your test-mode account when asked, and approve.
3. Confirm Stripe shows as connected.
Stripe's documentation describes its connector and what it can do; the page is linked in the Reseller Setup Walkthrough, lesson 13.2.
### 4. Add Clerk
1. Add the Clerk connector and sign in.
2. Select the application you created in lesson 1.
3. Some connectors need a separate authorization step before their tools appear. If Clerk says it needs authorization, finish that sign-in from the connector's entry in settings.
### 5. Test with a question that only reads
Open a new chat and paste:
 Using your Netlify, Stripe and Clerk connectors, list my Netlify sites, my Clerk application name, and my five most recent Stripe test payments. Do not change anything.

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Step by step.
A new account will show zero sites and zero payments. That is fine: you are checking that Claude reaches the right account, not that there is data. The answer should name your Clerk application and say "no sites" or list what you really have.

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Check yourself.
 [ ] All three connectors show as connected.
 [ ] The read-only test answered with facts from my own accounts.
 [ ] Nothing was changed by the test.

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — Keeping it safe
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / Keeping it safe.
 Approve narrowly. Choose your own team, your test-mode Stripe account, your one Clerk application.
 Read before write. Until you trust the setup, ask questions before you ask for changes.
 Know how to remove it. Each connector can be disconnected from the same settings, and from inside the service's own "authorized apps" page.
 Never paste secrets. If the chat asks for a secret key, stop: the connector should not need it. Say: "Do not ask me for secret keys. Tell me which dashboard setting to fill in."

chunks.title: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe — If something is off
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect Claude to Netlify, Clerk and Stripe / If something is off.
 A connector says it needs authorization. Its tools only appear after you complete sign-in; finish it from its entry in settings.
 The answer shows the wrong account. You signed in with a different account in the browser. Disconnect, sign out of the service, sign in with the right one and reconnect.
 Stripe shows live payments. You approved a live account. Disconnect and reconnect, choosing test mode.
Next: lesson 3, ChatGPT.

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way.
# Connect ChatGPT the same way
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: ChatGPT connected to your three services, or a clear decision to use Claude.
---

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Same idea, different menus
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Same idea, different menus.
ChatGPT can also use connectors built on the same open standard (the Model Context Protocol). The principles are identical to lesson 2: you sign in, you approve narrowly, you test with a question that only reads.
What differs is whether and where you can add them. That depends on your ChatGPT plan, on whether your workspace admin allows custom or third-party connectors, and on settings that OpenAI renames and moves from time to time. Because of that, start with OpenAI's current help page for connectors and apps, and treat anything below as the flow, not the exact button names.

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Do you need both assistants?
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Do you need both assistants?.
No. Pick one to do the build and stay with it, because a single conversation that knows your app is more useful than two that each know half. Many people keep the other as a second opinion for a stubborn error: paste the error message (never a secret) and ask for an independent explanation.
A reasonable choice:
 Use the assistant whose connectors worked first time on your plan.
 Use the other for review: "Here is the change my other assistant made. Explain what it does and tell me anything risky."

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Step by step.
1. Open ChatGPT, sign in, and look in settings for connectors or apps.
2. If your plan shows them, add Netlify, Stripe and Clerk, signing in to each with your own account and approving only your team, your test-mode Stripe account and your Clerk application.
3. If your plan does not show them, read OpenAI's help page for what is available to you. You can still follow the rest of the track: ask the assistant to explain each change and make the dashboard changes yourself, or do the build with Claude.
4. Run the same read-only test as lesson 2:
 Using your Netlify, Stripe and Clerk connectors, list my Netlify sites, my Clerk application name, and my five most recent Stripe test payments. Do not change anything.
5. Compare the answer with your three dashboards.

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Differences worth knowing
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Differences worth knowing.
 Some features are available only on certain plans or only in certain modes. If a feature is missing, it is usually the plan, not you.
 Connector tools may need to be explicitly switched on in each chat. If the chat says it cannot see Netlify, check that the connector is enabled for this conversation.
 Write actions (changing something) may ask for confirmation each time. Read the confirmation and approve only what you expect.

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Check yourself.
 [ ] I connected ChatGPT, or I confirmed my plan does not allow it and will use Claude.
 [ ] The read-only test returned my real data.
 [ ] I know how to disconnect each connector.

chunks.title: Connect ChatGPT the same way — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Connect ChatGPT the same way / Common mistakes.
 Copying a menu path from an old video. These menus move; use the official page.
 Assuming it works because it connected. Always run the read-only test.
 Giving broad access. Approve one team, one application, test mode.
Next: lesson 4, briefing your assistant on the app.

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app.
# Brief your assistant on the app
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: an assistant that has read your app, understands what it already includes, and has agreed to your working rules.
---

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — The assistant knows nothing about your app yet
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / The assistant knows nothing about your app yet.
Connected or not, a new chat does not know what your app is, where its code lives, what it already does or what you want. Most failed AI builds fail here: a vague request ("put my app online") produces vague, sometimes destructive, changes. A good briefing takes ten minutes and saves hours.
A good briefing has four parts.
### 1. Where the code is
Your own GitHub repository (the fork from the Reseller Setup Walkthrough). Not the original, and not someone else's.
### 2. What the app already includes
From your app's workshop page (the Overview, Accounts, Database and Environment panels):
 The framework: the reseller apps are Next.js applications.
 The database: PostgreSQL through Prisma, with the address in DATABASEURL.
 Sign-in: Google sign-in through NextAuth.
 Payments: Stripe checkout and a webhook that adds credits.
 AI: calls made with your MuAPI key.
Your workshop page lists the exact variable names for your app. Names only, never values.
### 3. What you want changed
For this track: host on Netlify, replace sign-in with Clerk, and keep the Stripe credits flow working in test mode.
### 4. How you want to work
 Small steps.
 Explain before changing.
 Separate branch for risky changes.
 Never ask for secret keys; say which dashboard setting to use.

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — The briefing
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / The briefing.
Copy this, fill in the three placeholders, and paste it into a new chat in the assistant you chose:
 I am building my own copy of a reseller app called <APP NAME. My code is in my GitHub repo <YOUR REPO ADDRESS. It already uses Next.js, Prisma with PostgreSQL, Stripe payments and Google sign-in through NextAuth. My goal: host it on Netlify, replace sign-in with Clerk, and keep the existing Stripe credits flow working in test mode. Work in small steps. Before each change, tell me what you will change and why, and wait for my approval. Make risky changes on a new branch. Never ask me to paste secret keys into this chat; tell me which dashboard setting to use instead. Start by reading the repo and summarising: how sign-in works, how payments and credits work, the build command, and every environment variable the code reads (names only).

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — Check the summary against the workshop page
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / Check the summary against the workshop page.
The assistant's summary is your first test. Compare it with your workshop panels:
 Does it name the same sign-in system (NextAuth with Google)?
 Does it find the Stripe webhook route and say what it does?
 Does it list the same environment variable names?
 Does it find where users and credits are stored?
If it gets something wrong, correct it now ("the webhook path is actually..."), because every later step builds on this understanding. If it cannot see your repo, use its GitHub connector or paste only the specific files it asks for, never anything containing a secret.

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — Setting expectations with the assistant
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / Setting expectations with the assistant.
After the summary, send:
 Good. For the rest of this project: always show me a plan first, change one thing at a time, tell me how to test each change, and tell me exactly which dashboard I must visit for anything involving a key or a setting.
This one message shapes the whole build.

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — Reading changes without being a developer
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / Reading changes without being a developer.
You will be asked to approve code changes. You do not need to understand every line. You do need to check three things:
1. Does the explanation match what I asked for? If you asked for Clerk sign-in and it is also rewriting payment code, stop and ask why.
2. Is it on a branch? Risky work belongs on a branch, so the working app is untouched until you merge.
3. Is there a test I can run? Every change should come with "open this page, you should see this".
If anything looks off, say so: "Explain that change in plain language and tell me what could go wrong."

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / Check yourself.
 [ ] The assistant correctly summarised my app.
 [ ] It agreed to explain before changing and not to ask for secrets.
 [ ] I corrected anything it got wrong.

chunks.title: Brief your assistant on the app — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Brief your assistant on the app / Common mistakes.
 Pasting secrets "to help". Never. The assistant does not need them to plan or to write code.
 Letting it make many changes at once. One change, one test.
 Skipping the summary check. A wrong assumption now becomes a broken build later.
Next: lesson 5, hosting on Netlify.

chunks.title: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site.
# Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: your app checked for Netlify and a Netlify site connected to your GitHub repo.
---

chunks.title: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site — What Netlify does
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site / What Netlify does.
Netlify connects to your GitHub repository. Every time you push a change, it builds the app (turns the code into something a browser can run) and publishes it. You do not run a server. If a build fails, nothing breaks: the previous working version keeps serving until a new one succeeds.
For a Next.js app, Netlify provides its own support for running Next.js features. Which settings you need (Node version, build command, plugin) can change between versions, so the assistant should check the current Netlify docs for Next.js rather than guess.

chunks.title: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site / Step by step.
### 1. Ask the assistant to check the app is ready
 Check this Next.js app is ready to deploy on Netlify, using the current Netlify docs for Next.js. List the build command, the Node version needed, and every environment variable the code reads (names only). Tell me about any change needed before I deploy, and wait for my approval before changing anything.
Compare the variable list with the Environment panel on your workshop page. They should match. Differences are worth a question: "Why does the code read X when my workshop page does not list it?"
### 2. Make any approved changes on a branch
If the assistant proposes a change (for example a Netlify configuration file, or a build setting), ask it to put it on a new branch named something like netlify-setup, and to explain it first. A typical result is a small configuration file; there should be no changes to your app's behaviour.
### 3. Create the site
Either:
 Ask the assistant to create the Netlify site from your GitHub repository through the connector, or
 Do it yourself: in Netlify choose to add a new project, import from GitHub, pick your repository and branch, and accept the build settings the assistant listed.
Doing it yourself the first time is a good way to learn where things are.

chunks.title: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site / Check yourself.
 [ ] The assistant listed the build command and every variable name, and it matches my workshop page.
 [ ] Any change was on a branch and explained first.
 [ ] A Netlify site exists, connected to my repository.

chunks.title: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Check your app is ready and create the Netlify site / Common mistakes.
 Accepting changes that alter the app's behaviour. Netlify setup should not change what the app does.
 Skipping the comparison with the workshop page.
Next: lesson 6, add variables, deploy and fix failures.

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures.
# Add variables, deploy and fix failures
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: your app live at a netlify.app address, with every secret in Netlify's settings and none in the chat or the code.
---

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures — Where secrets live
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures / Where secrets live.
Your app reads secrets (the database address, Stripe keys, the MuAPI key, Clerk keys later) from environment variables. The rule for the whole track:
 The assistant tells you the name of each variable.
 You paste the value into Netlify's environment variable settings.
 Values never go in the chat, the repository, a screenshot or an email.
After you add or change a variable, you must redeploy, because the app only reads variables when it is built or started.

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures / Step by step.
### 4. Add the environment variables
In your site's settings, find the environment variables area. For each variable name from your workshop page:
1. Add the name exactly as written.
2. Paste the value from the service that owns it (database host, Stripe, MuAPI).
3. Mark secrets as secret if Netlify offers the option.
Variables you do not have yet (Clerk keys, the Stripe webhook secret) come in lessons 8 and 10. The app will not be fully working until then; that is expected.
Two values need care:
 The site's public address variable (for example the one your app uses for its own URL) must match your real netlify.app address. You only know the address after the first deploy, so set it, then redeploy.
 Database address: use the connection string your database host gives for applications. If your host offers a "pooled" and a "direct" string, your workshop page says which variable takes which.
### 5. Deploy
Trigger a deploy and watch the log. A successful deploy ends with a status such as Published. Open the address.
### 6. If the deploy fails
Do not guess. Ask:
 Read the failed deploy log through the Netlify connector and tell me the first error and what causes it. Do not change anything yet.
Then fix one error at a time, redeploying after each. The first error is usually the real one; later errors are often consequences.

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures — What "working" looks like at this stage
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures / What "working" looks like at this stage.
 The home page loads.
 Pages that do not need sign-in or payments work.
 Sign-in may not work yet (lessons 7 to 9 replace it) and payments are not connected to your Netlify address yet (lesson 10). That is fine.

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures / Check yourself.
 [ ] The deploy shows Published.
 [ ] My netlify.app address opens my app's home page.
 [ ] All variables I have so far are in Netlify, none in the chat or the repository.
 [ ] I redeployed after adding variables.

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures / Common mistakes.
 Changing a variable and not redeploying. Nothing changes until the next deploy.
 A typo in a variable name. Names must match exactly, including capitals.
 Putting secrets in a file in the repo. Even a private repo is not the place.
 Fixing several errors at once. You will not know which fix worked.

chunks.title: Add variables, deploy and fix failures — If something is off
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Add variables, deploy and fix failures / If something is off.
 Build fails on a missing variable. The build reads it. Add it in Netlify and redeploy.
 The page loads but data fails. The database address is wrong or the tables were not created. Revisit Module 5 of the Reseller Setup Walkthrough.
 Works locally but not on Netlify. The assistant should compare the Node version and build command with Netlify's settings.
Next: lesson 7, planning the Clerk change.

chunks.title: Plan the Clerk change
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Plan the Clerk change.
# Plan the Clerk change
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a reviewed plan for replacing NextAuth with Clerk that keeps every person's credits.
---

chunks.title: Plan the Clerk change — What changes and what must not
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Plan the Clerk change / What changes and what must not.
Your app ships with Google sign-in through NextAuth. Clerk replaces it with ready-made sign-up and sign-in screens, email and Google options, and a dashboard where you can see your users. This is a real change to your copy of the code, so we do it carefully.
What must not break: the link between a person and their credits. Your app stores users and credits in its own database. If Clerk creates a new user identity and the app does not connect it to a user record, every new sign-up will have no credits (or worse, someone sees another person's). So the plan comes before the code.

chunks.title: Plan the Clerk change — How Clerk works, in plain terms
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Plan the Clerk change / How Clerk works, in plain terms.
 Clerk keeps the account (email, password or Google, sessions).
 Your app asks Clerk, on every request, "who is signed in?" and gets a user ID.
 Your app uses that ID to find, or create, its own user record and its credits.
Clerk gives you two keys:
 A publishable key: safe to be visible in the browser.
 A secret key: private; it goes only in Netlify's environment variables.
Clerk's official docs describe adding it to Next.js and also describe tools for working with AI assistants. Always ask your assistant to follow the current Clerk docs rather than from memory, because the exact setup changes between versions.

chunks.title: Plan the Clerk change — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Plan the Clerk change / Step by step.
### 1. Plan before any change
 Plan how to replace NextAuth with Clerk in this app using the current Clerk docs for Next.js. Show me where users and credits are stored, how each Clerk user will map to a user record in our database, what happens to people who already signed in with Google, and the exact files you will change. Do not change anything yet.
Read the plan for these points:
 A mapping. It should say how a Clerk user ID is stored against a user record, and how a new user gets starting credits (if the app gives any).
 Existing users. If you already have customers, ask how they keep their credits. A new app with no customers can ignore this.
 Files. The list should be about sign-in, middleware and the user lookup, not payments or AI calls.
If the plan touches payment code, ask why.

chunks.title: Plan the Clerk change — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Plan the Clerk change / Check yourself.
 [ ] I read the plan and it maps Clerk users to user records and credits.
 [ ] It says what happens to existing users (or I have none).
 [ ] The file list is about sign-in and users, not payments or AI calls.

chunks.title: Plan the Clerk change — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Plan the Clerk change / Common mistakes.
 Approving a plan that touches payment code without asking why.
 Skipping the plan and asking for the change directly.
Next: lesson 8, make the change and add the keys.

chunks.title: Make the Clerk change and add the keys
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Make the Clerk change and add the keys.
# Make the Clerk change and add the keys
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: Clerk working on a Netlify preview deploy, with the keys in Netlify only.
---
Your plan from lesson 7 is approved. Now the assistant makes the change on a separate branch, and you add the Clerk keys yourself.

chunks.title: Make the Clerk change and add the keys — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Make the Clerk change and add the keys / Step by step.
### 2. Make the change on a branch
 Create a branch called clerk-signup and make the change you described. Explain each file you change. Tell me the exact environment variable names I need to add in Netlify. Do not ask me for secret keys.
### 3. Add the Clerk keys in Netlify
1. In Clerk, open the API keys page for your development instance.
2. In Netlify, open your site's environment variable settings.
3. Add the variable names the assistant gave you, pasting the publishable and secret keys yourself.
4. Redeploy the branch as a deploy preview (Netlify can build a preview for a branch).

chunks.title: Make the Clerk change and add the keys — Development instance vs production
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Make the Clerk change and add the keys / Development instance vs production.
Clerk's development instance is for building and testing. It works on netlify.app and preview addresses. A production instance requires your own domain and its own keys, and it is a separate set of users. You will set that up when you go live in lesson 13; do not use it earlier.

chunks.title: Make the Clerk change and add the keys — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Make the Clerk change and add the keys / Check yourself.
 [ ] The change is on a branch called clerk-signup.
 [ ] Each changed file was explained to me.
 [ ] Clerk keys are in Netlify only.
 [ ] A preview deploy of the branch built successfully.

chunks.title: Make the Clerk change and add the keys — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Make the Clerk change and add the keys / Common mistakes.
 Putting the Clerk secret key in code or chat.
 Forgetting to redeploy after adding the keys.
 Using the production instance too early.
Next: lesson 9, test sign-up and merge.

chunks.title: Test sign-up and merge
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test sign-up and merge.
# Test sign-up and merge
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: Clerk handling sign-up and sign-in, tested with a fresh account, with each person's credits correct, and the branch merged.
---
Test on the preview deploy from lesson 8. Only merge when every check passes.

chunks.title: Test sign-up and merge — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test sign-up and merge / Step by step.
### 4. Test with a fresh account
1. Open the preview address in a private window.
2. Use sign-up with a new test email address (an alias you control is fine).
3. Complete any email verification Clerk asks for.
4. You should land in the app, signed in.
5. In Clerk's dashboard, open Users. Your test user should be listed.
6. In the app, check credits. A new user should have exactly what a new user should have.
7. Sign out and sign back in. You should return to the same account and the same credits.
### 5. Also test the edge cases
 Sign in with Google if you enabled it.
 Visit a page that needs sign-in while signed out. You should be sent to sign-in, not shown an error.
 Visit the sign-in page while signed in. You should be sent on into the app.
### 6. Merge when it works
Only merge the branch once every test above passes. If something fails, describe exactly what you saw to the assistant ("I signed up, landed on the dashboard, but credits show zero") and fix one thing at a time.

chunks.title: Test sign-up and merge — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test sign-up and merge / Check yourself.
 [ ] A fresh test sign-up works, appears in Clerk and has correct credits.
 [ ] I only merged after every test passed.

chunks.title: Test sign-up and merge — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test sign-up and merge / Common mistakes.
 Merging before testing a fresh sign-up. Existing sessions hide problems.
 Putting the Clerk secret key in code or chat.
 Forgetting to redeploy after adding the keys.
 Using the production instance too early.
 Letting the assistant change payment code as part of this step.

chunks.title: Test sign-up and merge — If something is off
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test sign-up and merge / If something is off.
 Sign-up works but credits are missing. The new Clerk user is not linked to a user record. Ask the assistant to create or look up the record the first time a user is seen, and to show you where.
 Sign-in fails on the preview address. Check that you are using the development instance keys and that the allowed addresses in Clerk include your preview address. Ask the assistant to check the current Clerk docs.
 Redirect loop. Often a middleware setting. Ask the assistant to read the middleware and explain which routes are public.
Next: lesson 10, Stripe keys and the webhook.

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook.
# Stripe keys and the webhook
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: your Stripe test keys and a webhook endpoint connected to your Netlify site.
---

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook — Stripe is already built in
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook / Stripe is already built in.
You are not adding payments. The app already creates Stripe checkouts for credit packs and already has a webhook that listens for completed payments and adds credits. All you do is connect your Stripe account to your deployment: keys, then a webhook that points at your address.
If you did Modules 7 to 9 of the Reseller Setup Walkthrough for Vercel, this is the same set of steps on a different host.

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook — How a payment flows
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook / How a payment flows.
1. A customer clicks a credit pack. Your app sends them to Stripe Checkout.
2. They pay on Stripe's page (in test mode: a test card).
3. Stripe sends your app a webhook: a message to a specific address saying "this checkout completed".
4. Your app checks the message is really from Stripe (using the signing secret), then adds the credits.
The two things people get wrong are the webhook address and the signing secret. Your workshop page's webhook panel gives the exact path your app listens on.

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook — Test mode, strictly
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook / Test mode, strictly.
Stay in test mode. Stripe's test cards never charge anyone, and test and live data are completely separate: a test key cannot see live payments and vice versa. Going live is lesson 13, not now.

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook / Step by step.
### 1. Add the Stripe test keys to Netlify
1. In Stripe (test mode) open the API keys page.
2. In Netlify's environment variable settings, add the Stripe variables named in your workshop page, pasting the test values yourself.
3. If your app also uses a publishable key in the browser, add it the same way.
### 2. Create the webhook
1. In Stripe's webhook settings (test mode), add an endpoint.
2. The address is your netlify.app address plus the webhook path from your workshop page.
3. Listen for the event checkout.session.completed.
4. After creating it, Stripe shows a signing secret. Copy it into the Netlify variable your workshop page names for it.
5. Redeploy. The new variable is only picked up on the next deploy.

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook / Check yourself.
 [ ] Stripe test keys and the webhook signing secret are in Netlify only.
 [ ] The webhook address is my netlify.app address plus the path from my workshop page, listening for checkout.session.completed.
 [ ] I redeployed after adding them.

chunks.title: Stripe keys and the webhook — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Stripe keys and the webhook / Common mistakes.
 A live key during testing. Test mode only until the go-live lessons.
 A webhook address with the wrong path (or a trailing slash that does not match).
 Using the wrong secret. Each endpoint has its own signing secret.
Next: lesson 11, test purchase and check it from the chat.

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat.
# Test purchase and check it from the chat
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a test purchase that adds credits, confirmed by your assistant from Stripe.
---
Your keys and webhook are in place from lesson 10. Now prove the whole payment path works.

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat — Step by step
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat / Step by step.
### 3. Make a test purchase
1. Sign in to your app (Clerk, from lessons 7 to 9).
2. Buy a credit pack.
3. On Stripe's page use the test card from Stripe's testing documentation, with any future expiry and any security code.
4. You should return to your app and see your credits increase.
### 4. Ask the assistant to verify from Stripe
 Using the Stripe connector in test mode, find my most recent test checkout session and tell me whether it succeeded, and whether the webhook delivery to my site returned a success response. Do not change anything.
This turns "it seems to work" into evidence: the payment succeeded and the webhook reached your app.
### 5. Test the unhappy paths
 Use Stripe's test card for a declined payment. Credits must not change.
 Cancel on the Checkout page. You should come back to the app with no credits added.
 Check that buying twice adds credits twice, not once or four times.

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat — What good looks like
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat / What good looks like.
 Stripe's dashboard shows the test payment as succeeded.
 The webhook endpoint shows a successful delivery.
 Your credits increased by exactly the pack size.

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat / Check yourself.
 [ ] A test purchase added the right credits.
 [ ] The assistant confirmed the payment and webhook delivery from Stripe.
 [ ] A declined card added nothing.

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat / Common mistakes.
 A live key during testing. Test mode only until lesson 13.
 Not redeploying after adding the signing secret.
 A webhook address with the wrong path (or a trailing slash that does not match).
 Using the wrong secret. Each webhook endpoint has its own signing secret; copy the one for this endpoint.

chunks.title: Test purchase and check it from the chat — If something is off
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Test purchase and check it from the chat / If something is off.
 Payment succeeded but credits did not appear. The webhook failed. Ask the assistant to read the delivery result in Stripe. Common causes: wrong address, wrong signing secret, or an unredeployed variable.
 The webhook returns an error. Ask the assistant to read the response and the app's logs on Netlify, and explain the first error.
 Credits added to the wrong person. Stop and ask the assistant to check how the checkout session is tied to a user; this usually comes from a mapping error in lessons 7 to 9.
Next: lesson 12, save your prompts and run the customer test.

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test.
# Save your prompts and run the customer test
 Time: about 15 minutes. You will finish with: a reusable checklist, your saved prompts and a passing customer test on your Netlify address.
---

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test — The whole path in one page
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test / The whole path in one page.
| Step | Lessons | You do | The assistant does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Accounts | 1 | Create Netlify, Clerk, Stripe (test) | Nothing yet |
| Connect | 2 or 3 | Approve connectors | Reads your accounts |
| Brief | 4 | Paste the briefing, check the summary | Summarises the app |
| Host | 5 and 6 | Add variable values, deploy | Checks readiness, explains errors |
| Sign-up | 7 to 9 | Add Clerk keys, test a fresh account | Plans and changes the code on a branch |
| Payments | 10 and 11 | Add Stripe keys and webhook, buy a pack | Verifies payment and webhook |
| Launch | 12 and 13 | Domain, live keys, final test | Produces the go-live checklist |
What changes from app to app is only the facts on its workshop page: the name, the database, the variable names. The prompts stay the same, which is why saving them matters.

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test — Save your prompts
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test / Save your prompts.
Make a note titled "Launch prompts" and paste in:
1. The briefing from lesson 4.
2. The deploy-readiness prompt from lesson 5.
3. The Clerk plan prompt from lesson 7.
4. The Stripe verification prompt from lesson 11.
5. The go-live prompt from lesson 13.
For the next app you replace the app name and repo address and go straight down the list.

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test — Branding, domain and the customer test
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test / Branding, domain and the customer test.
Before you go live, finish the business side with Modules 10 and 11 of the Reseller Setup Walkthrough: your app's name and logo, your own domain, and the full customer test (sign up, buy, use the app, see credits). Run that test on your Netlify address and again on your domain.

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test — Keeping it healthy
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test / Keeping it healthy.
 Check Stripe and Netlify weekly for failed webhooks and failed deploys. Ask the assistant: "Summarise failed deploys and failed webhook deliveries from the last 7 days."
 Watch your free-plan limits on Netlify and Clerk as users grow.
 Rotate a key if it was ever exposed, then redeploy.
 Back up your database per your host's guidance.
 Never let the assistant change live data without a plan you have read.

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test / Check yourself.
 [ ] I saved my reusable prompts.
 [ ] I ran the full customer test on the Netlify address.

chunks.title: Save your prompts and run the customer test — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Save your prompts and run the customer test / Common mistakes.
 Skipping the customer test because each step worked on its own.
Next: lesson 13, go live.

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live.
# Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live
 Time: about 18 minutes. You will finish with: your app live on your own domain with Clerk production and Stripe live mode, tested with a real payment you refunded.
---

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live — Going live deliberately
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live / Going live deliberately.
Going live changes three things at once, and each has a separate "live" version that does not carry over from test:
1. Your domain. Add it in Netlify and follow its DNS instructions. Netlify serves the site on the new address once DNS settles.
2. Clerk production instance. Clerk's production instance needs your own domain and has its own keys and its own (empty) user list. Create it, add its keys to Netlify's production environment variables, and redeploy.
3. Stripe live mode. Activate your account (Module 7 of the walkthrough), create live keys, create a live webhook for your real address, and put the live signing secret in Netlify.
Ask the assistant to build the checklist for your specific app:
 Give me a go-live checklist for this app on Netlify with Clerk and Stripe: custom domain, Clerk production instance, live Stripe keys, live webhook, environment variables per environment, and a final test. Mark each item as either "I do this in a dashboard" or "you change this in the code". Do not change anything.
### The final test
1. Sign up with a new real email on your domain.
2. Buy the smallest credit pack with a real card.
3. Confirm credits arrive and Stripe shows the payment and a successful webhook.
4. Refund the payment yourself in Stripe and check it behaves as your Module 9 plan says.
Do this once, deliberately, before you tell anyone the app is live.

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live — Check yourself
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live / Check yourself.
 [ ] I have a go-live checklist for this specific app.
 [ ] I understand that domain, Clerk production and Stripe live are three separate switches.

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live — Common mistakes
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live / Common mistakes.
 Going live without a final end-to-end test.
 Carrying test keys into production (or live keys into preview builds).
 Forgetting the live webhook. The test one does not work for live payments.
 Not refunding your own test purchase.

chunks.title: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live — If something is off
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Go live: domain, Clerk production and Stripe live / If something is off.
 It worked on the preview but not on my domain. Production variables, the Clerk production instance and the Stripe live webhook are separate from test. Check each one.
 Sign-in fails only on my domain. The Clerk production instance may not list the domain yet.
 A payment succeeded but nothing happened. Check the live webhook's recent deliveries.
You now have the full process. Repeat it for every app you launch, and use Module 12 of the Reseller Setup Walkthrough to find and win your first customers.

chunks.title: Track 1: AI Video Ads & UGC
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: Track 1: AI Video Ads & UGC.
# Track 1: AI Video Ads & UGC
 SmartVideo GO AI Academy — Part of the SmartVideo GO AI course library. Everything in this lesson can be produced end-to-end inside SmartVideo GO AI using its Image, Video, Audio, Cinema, Lip-Sync, Storyboard, VFX, Thumbnail and AI Influencer studios, plus the Create-With-AI recipe system.
 Turn AI-generated video into ads brands actually pay for.
Five modules, in order. Each is one markdown file — click straight in, no subfolders. Every module follows the same structure: Problem → Concept → Do It → Compare Tools → Launch It → Exercises.
"Templates" below = the reusable template(s) each module produces (a script template, checklist, pricing sheet) — actual files you fill in and reuse, saved in templates/.
| # | Module | Time | Requires |
|:---:|---|:---:|---|
| 1 | How AI UGC Actually Works | ~45 min | — |
| 2 | Character & Face Consistency | ~40 min | Module 1 |

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works.
# How AI UGC Actually Works
 SmartVideo GO AI Academy — Part of the SmartVideo GO AI course library. Everything in this lesson can be produced end-to-end inside SmartVideo GO AI using its Image, Video, Audio, Cinema, Lip-Sync, Storyboard, VFX, Thumbnail and AI Influencer studios, plus the Create-With-AI recipe system.
 A UGC ad is just five pieces stitched together — once you can see the seams, you can make any of them.
Track: AI Video Ads & UGC
Time: ~45 minutes
Prerequisites: None

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — The Problem
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / The Problem.
Brands pay real creators $200-$1,500 per UGC (user-generated-content-style) ad because it converts better than polished studio ads — it looks like a real person talking to camera about a product, not a commercial. The problem: sourcing, briefing, filming, and revising human creators is slow, and it doesn't scale. A brand that wants 20 ad variants to test can't get 20 creators on short notice.
AI-generated UGC solves the scaling problem, but most people trying it get stuck on one thing: their AI "creator" doesn't look consistent from shot to shot, or the voice/lip-sync looks obviously fake, and the ad gets rejected. Understanding the actual pipeline — not just "type a prompt" — is what separates a usable ad from an uncanny one.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — The Concept
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / The Concept.
A UGC-style AI ad is five stages, each producible independently and swappable:
Script → Avatar / Voice → Video → Captions → Export
- Script — a short, conversational hook + pitch + call-to-action, written the way a real person talks, not ad copy.
- Avatar/Voice — either a generated talking-head avatar with a cloned/synthetic voice, or a still reference image animated with lip-sync driven by an audio track.
- Video — the avatar's performance, plus any b-roll (product shots, screen recordings) cut around it.
- Captions — auto-generated, burned-in captions, standard for the format because most viewers watch muted.
- Export — format/aspect ratio matched to the platform (9:16 for Reels/TikTok/Shorts, sometimes 1:1 or 16:9).
The reason this pipeline matters more than any single "best model" is that each stage can be produced by a different tool, and the weak link is whichever stage looks least real — usually the avatar's face/voice sync, not the script or captions.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Do It.
1. Write the script. Keep it under 30 seconds spoken (~75-90 words). Structure: hook (first 2 seconds — a question, a bold claim, or a visual surprise), problem/pitch (10-15 seconds), proof or demo (10-15 seconds), call-to-action (last 2-3 seconds).
2. Generate the voice. Use a text-to-speech or voice-cloning model to turn the script into natural-sounding narration. Match tone to the product (energetic for a gadget, calm for skincare) — and don't stop at the first take. Generate 2-3 versions varying pacing and emphasis (which word gets stressed in the hook line changes how "surprised" or "casual" it reads), and pick the one that sounds least like it's being read off a page. Accent/demographic match to the product's likely audience matters here too — a mismatched voice can undercut an otherwise good script.
3. Generate or animate the avatar. Either generate a talking-head video directly from the script/voice, or animate a reference image with lip-sync driven by the audio track.
4. Add b-roll. Cut in product shots or screen recordings during the pitch/proof section — this also hides any short imperfect stretches in the avatar footage.
5. Caption and export. Auto-generate captions, burn them in, and export at 9:16 for short-form platforms.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Do It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Do It.
6. Ship check. Before sending anything to a client, watch the finished ad once with sound off (does the hook work from captions alone?) and once with sound on at regular volume. If you catch yourself pausing anywhere to figure out what's happening, a client will too — that's a sign to fix pacing or cut, not just ship it and see.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Worked Example
chunks.text: Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Worked Example.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Worked Example
chunks.text: Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Worked Example. - Proof/Demo (15-25s): a visual demo (slapping the phone on) plus a concrete duration ("two weeks, potholes included") — specific numbers read as more credible than "it works great." - CTA (25-28s): price stated plainly, one action ("link's below"), urgency tied to a real use case (road trip) instead of a generic "buy now." Why this script would survive production: it's short enough to keep energy up on one take, the demo moment (slapping the phone on) gives the avatar something to do with its hands instead of just talking — which also hides minor avatar imperfections — and it never says "AI" or sounds scripted. Common first-attempt mistake: writing the pitch section like copy ("Introducing GripMount, the revolutionary new way to...") instead of like speech. Read your script out loud before producing anything — if you wouldn't say it to a friend, rewrite it. The clip below is real, not a mockup — the anchor image from Module 2 animated into a short talking clip from the hook line above, so you can see what a first-pass output actually looks like before any editing/b-roll/captions are added:

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Worked Example
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Worked Example.
How this was actually produced, end to end, via the muapi API:
1. Generated the anchor portrait with nano-banana-2 (text-to-image, $0.06/image) — the same image used in Module 2's example.
2. Uploaded that image via muapi's uploadfile endpoint to get a URL the next model could reference.
3. Fed that image URL into seedance-2-image-to-video-fast (image-to-video, $0.75/clip) with a prompt describing the action and the exact line of dialogue — no separate TTS/lip-sync pass was needed, since this model generates speech and mouth movement together from the prompt.
4. Downloaded the resulting .mp4 from muapi's CDN (generated outputs expire after 30 days, so anything you want to keep needs downloading promptly) and converted it to the silent GIF preview above with ffmpeg for inline display.
Total cost for this one clip: $0.81 across the two model calls. This is exactly the "image → video model, prompt-driven" pipeline described in Do It, step 3 — the models named here are current examples, not a fixed recommendation; see Compare Tools below for how to pick a model when these become outdated.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Compare Tools
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Compare Tools.
Model names change constantly, but the category choice matters more than any specific model — here's what's actually reasonable for each stage right now:
| Stage | Good muapi models to reach for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Voice/TTS | Gemini TTS, ElevenLabs text-to-dialogue | Natural multi-speaker delivery with emotion/pace control — not robotic TTS |
| Avatar/video (image → talking clip) | Seedance 2.x, Kling 3.0 | Current-generation video models that handle head/hand motion and speech convincingly in one pass, as in the clip above |
| Lip-sync (audio-driven, onto an existing video/image) | A dedicated lip-sync model (e.g. sync-style lip-sync) or a Kling avatar model | Better fit when you already have separately-recorded narration you need to match to a face, rather than generating speech+motion together |
| Path | Cost per ad | Setup effort | Consistency | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| muapi API (managed) | Per-generation credit cost, no infra | Low — call the endpoint, get a result | High — same model/voice reused via API params | Fast iteration, client work, testing many variants |
| Other paid all-in-one UGC tools | Often subscription-gated, per-seat pricing | Low, but locked to their UI/workflow | Varies by tool | Teams that want a GUI, not an API |

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Compare Tools
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Compare Tools.
| Local/self-hosted (ComfyUI + local TTS/video models, e.g. LTX 2.3) | Free after hardware, but needs a capable GPU | High — workflow setup, model downloads, tuning | Can be very high once tuned, but slower to get there | Zero marginal cost at volume, full control, privacy-sensitive clients who don't want cloud processing |
LTX 2.3 is worth naming specifically for the local path: it's an open-weight video model runnable in ComfyUI, so it's the closest local equivalent to the Seedance/Kling-class models above — weaker out of the box, but the only one of this group you can actually run on your own GPU instead of an API call.
The honest tradeoff: local is genuinely free per-generation once set up, but the setup and iteration time cost is real — expect to spend a weekend tuning a ComfyUI workflow before it's reliable. API is the right default while you're still learning what "good" looks like; local becomes worth it once you're producing at real volume (dozens of ads/month) or a client specifically needs on-premise generation.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Launch It
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Launch It.
How to price it: Individual UGC-style ad gigs on freelance marketplaces run roughly $10-$55 per finished ad; agencies retainer this work at $1,500-$3,000/month for ongoing batches. Price by deliverable (e.g., "$150 for 5 ad variants") rather than by hour — clients understand ad packages, not your production time.
How to position it: Lead with the business outcome ("more ad variants to test, faster, without a film crew"), not the AI process. Brands buying UGC ads care about conversion and testing speed, not how the video was made.
Where to find first clients: DTC e-commerce brands running paid social ads are the best fit — they already buy UGC and already understand the format. Cold outreach to brands you can see running Meta/TikTok ads (visible in the platforms' public ad libraries) with a sample ad for their actual product is a stronger opener than a generic pitch.
The real numbers: Documented case studies show individual brands running AI-UGC-style creative at $600K+/month in ad spend for a single product — the point isn't that you'll match that, it's that the format is proven at scale, not a novelty.

chunks.title: How AI UGC Actually Works — Exercises
chunks.text:
Academy lesson: How AI UGC Actually Works / Exercises.
1. Easy: Write three 30-second UGC scripts for a product you use, following the hook/pitch/proof/CTA structure.
2. Medium: Produce one full ad end-to-end (script → voice → avatar → captions → export) for a real or hypothetical product.
3. Hard: Produce 5 variants of the same ad (same product, different hooks or angles) and compare which hook you'd expect to perform best, and why.
